title: The Critical Importance of Retrieval for Learning
authors: Karpicke, J. D., & Roediger, H. L.
design: Between-subjects laboratory experiment with four learning conditions (repeated study-test, repeated study only after learning, repeated test only after learning, dropped from both)
population: Undergraduate students at Washington University in St. Louis learning Swahili-English vocabulary word pairs
institution: Washington University in St. Louis, Department of Psychology
outcome: Continued retrieval practice after items were first learned produced far greater one-week retention (about 80%) than continued restudying with no further testing (about a third), even though repeated studying after initial learning had no additional benefit on delayed recall.
limitations: The four learning conditions were compared between subjects (16 per group) rather than within subjects, a design later noted by other researchers to confound the spacing of study/test opportunities across groups, and the task used simple foreign-vocabulary paired associates rather than more complex, meaningful materials.
qualityRationale: Controlled between-subjects laboratory experiment with a clear causal manipulation and objective recall outcomes, published in Science; graded B rather than A because of the modest per-cell N (16) and a between-subjects design later shown to carry a spacing confound.

title: Retrieval Practice Produces More Learning than Elaborative Studying with Concept Mapping
authors: Karpicke, J. D., & Blunt, J. R.
design: Randomized between-subjects laboratory experiment (Experiment 1) comparing single study, repeated study, elaborative concept mapping, and retrieval practice conditions
population: Undergraduate students at Purdue University studying a short expository science text
institution: Purdue University, Department of Psychological Sciences
outcome: Students who practiced free-recall retrieval after reading a science text scored about one and a half standard deviations higher on a final short-answer test one week later than students who studied the same text using elaborative concept mapping, even though students themselves predicted concept mapping would produce better learning.
limitations: Students in the concept-mapping condition had no prior training or experience constructing concept maps before the experiment, so the study could not rule out that experienced concept-mappers would benefit more from that strategy; this point was directly disputed in a published comment on the study.
qualityRationale: Randomized controlled laboratory experiment with random assignment across four conditions, an objective delayed outcome measure, and internal replication across two experiments in the same paper, published in Science.

title: Test-Enhanced Learning in the Classroom: Long-Term Improvements From Quizzing
authors: Roediger, H. L., Agarwal, P. K., McDaniel, M. A., & McDermott, K. B.
design: Quasi-experimental classroom field study across three experiments conducted within real sixth-grade social-studies units, comparing quizzed versus non-quizzed material
population: Sixth-grade students at Columbia Middle School, Columbia, Illinois, taking a social studies course
institution: Washington University in St. Louis, Department of Psychology
outcome: Material that had been quizzed with clicker or short-answer questions during the semester was recalled better on unit exams and on the cumulative end-of-semester exam than material that was reviewed but never quizzed.
limitations: Only one of the three experiments (Experiment 2) included a restudy control condition, and the advantage of quizzing over restudying, visible on the immediate chapter exam, was no longer reliably present by the cumulative end-of-semester exam.
qualityRationale: Real classroom quasi-experiment spanning a full semester with objective exam outcomes and three replicating experiments, but material-to-be-quizzed assignment was not a fully randomized controlled trial and the data come from a single school and subject area.

title: Spacing Effects in Learning: A Temporal Ridgeline of Optimal Retention
authors: Cepeda, N. J., Vul, E., Rohrer, D., Wixted, J. T., & Pashler, H.
design: Large-scale web-based experiment systematically manipulating inter-study interval and retention interval across 26 conditions
population: Adult volunteers recruited over the internet who studied and were tested on trivia-type facts
institution: University of California, San Diego (Vul, Wixted, Pashler); York University (Cepeda); University of South Florida (Rohrer)
outcome: Final-test performance depended jointly on the gap between study sessions and the delay before the final test: for any given retention interval, increasing the inter-study gap first improved and then reduced final recall, with the optimal gap falling from roughly 20-40% of a short retention interval to about 5-10% for a one-year retention interval.
limitations: Participants were self-selected volunteers who completed the study online rather than a randomly sampled or classroom-based population, and the to-be-learned materials were relatively simple trivia facts rather than curriculum content, limiting direct generalization to school-based learning.
qualityRationale: Very large sample (N=1,350) with systematic experimental manipulation of both spacing and retention interval across 26 conditions, providing a precise dose-response mapping of the spacing effect; graded A for scale and experimental control despite self-selected online recruitment.

title: Optimising learning using flashcards: Spacing is more effective than cramming
authors: Kornell, N.
design: Within-subjects laboratory experiment (Experiment 1 of three) comparing spaced versus massed flashcard study using a self-paced, web-based study program
population: UCLA undergraduate students studying GRE-type synonym word pairs
institution: University of California, Los Angeles, Department of Psychology
outcome: Across three experiments, spacing flashcard study of vocabulary pairs across sessions produced better final recall than massing (cramming) study into fewer, larger sessions for the large majority of participants (about 90%), even though most participants believed massing had been more effective.
limitations: The task used artificial GRE-style paired-associate vocabulary rather than authentic classroom curriculum, and study was self-paced on a computer rather than embedded in an actual course, leaving open how far the size of the spacing advantage transfers to real classroom study.
qualityRationale: Controlled within-subjects lab experiment replicated across three experiments with a clear behavioral outcome, but individual-experiment samples were modest (e.g., 25 participants in Experiment 1) and drawn from a single university subject pool.

title: Maintenance of Foreign Language Vocabulary and the Spacing Effect
authors: Bahrick, H. P., Bahrick, L. E., Bahrick, A. S., & Bahrick, P. E.
design: 9-year within-subjects longitudinal training experiment manipulating relearning-session interval (13 vs. 26 sessions spaced 14, 28, or 56 days apart) and testing retention 1-5 years after training ended
population: Four members of the Bahrick family (the study's own investigators), who learned and relearned 300 English-foreign-language word pairs
institution: Ohio Wesleyan University; Florida International University
outcome: Longer spacing between relearning sessions slowed initial acquisition slightly but produced substantially better long-term retention, such that 13 relearning sessions spaced 56 days apart yielded retention comparable to 26 sessions spaced only 14 days apart.
limitations: The study used only 4 participants, who were the investigators' own family members rather than a randomly recruited sample, sharply limiting statistical power and generalizability to the broader population even though the within-subject design spanned an unusually long 9-year period.
qualityRationale: Tightly controlled, unusually long (9-year) repeated-measures training experiment with objective recall outcomes, but graded B rather than A because the sample consists of only 4 non-randomly-selected family members, sharply limiting external validity.

title: The shuffling of mathematics problems improves learning
authors: Rohrer, D., & Taylor, K.
design: Controlled laboratory experiment (two experiments) with random assignment to blocked/massed vs. shuffled/mixed and spaced practice schedules
population: College students learning to solve mathematics problems (volume-of-solid problem type)
outcome: Across two experiments, practice using a shuffled (mixed/interleaved and spaced) problem format produced far higher scores on a test given about one week later than practice using the standard blocked/massed format; performance was described as vastly superior after mixed practice.
limitations: Both experiments used a single, narrow mathematics task (calculating the number of sides of a solid) practiced in one or two lab-like sessions with college students, so the design does not establish how the effect generalizes to real multi-topic classroom instruction over a school term.
qualityRationale: Controlled lab experiment with random assignment across two studies, but single-session, single-task-type, non-classroom design with a moderate sample.

title: Interleaved practice improves mathematics learning
authors: Rohrer, D., Dedrick, R. F., & Stershic, S.
design: Cluster-randomized controlled trial in real classrooms comparing interleaved vs. blocked assignment ordering over a three-month period
population: Seventh-grade students in Florida public middle school mathematics classes
institution: University of South Florida (in partnership with Hillsborough County Public Schools, Florida)
outcome: Compared to blocked practice, interleaved practice produced higher scores on both an immediate test and a test delayed by about one month (Cohen's d = 0.42 and 0.79, respectively).
limitations: The study examined only middle-school mathematics content within one district over one semester, so the size and durability of the interleaving benefit for other subjects, age groups, or longer time spans was not directly tested.
qualityRationale: Cluster-randomized controlled trial conducted in authentic classrooms over a multi-month intervention, independently reviewed by the What Works Clearinghouse as meeting standards without reservations.

title: Why interleaving enhances inductive learning: The roles of discrimination and retrieval
authors: Birnbaum, M. S., Kornell, N., Bjork, E. L., & Bjork, R. A.
design: Three controlled laboratory experiments manipulating blocked vs. interleaved presentation of category exemplars and spacing
population: UCLA undergraduate students (32 in Experiment 1, 40 in Experiment 2, 48 in Experiment 3)
outcome: Interleaving photographs of different bird/butterfly categories improved participants' later discrimination between categories relative to blocked study; temporal spacing was only beneficial when it did not disrupt the direct juxtaposition of to-be-discriminated categories, supporting a discriminative-contrast account of the interleaving benefit.
limitations: The experiments relied on artificial, unfamiliar visual categories (bird and butterfly species) learned by undergraduates in brief single-session lab tasks, limiting generalizability to real classroom category learning over longer timescales.
qualityRationale: Well-controlled multi-experiment lab study with random assignment, but modest per-cell sample sizes and artificial stimuli typical of basic cognitive-psychology lab work rather than a large-scale field RCT.

title: Training strategies for attaining transfer of problem-solving skill in statistics: A cognitive-load approach
authors: Paas, F. G. W. C.
design: Controlled experiment comparing conventional problem-solving practice against worked-example and problem-completion (partially worked-out) training strategies
population: Dutch secondary school students (45 male, 1 female)
institution: University of Twente, Department of Instructional Technology, Netherlands
outcome: Students trained with worked examples and, especially, with the problem-completion strategy achieved better transfer performance and invested less mental effort than students who practiced with conventional problem solving, supporting a cognitive-load explanation of the advantage.
limitations: The sample was small and heavily skewed toward male participants (45 of 46), and the task domain (statistics problems) and single-session design limit generalization to other subjects, longer training periods, and more balanced populations.
qualityRationale: Controlled lab/classroom experiment with random assignment to training strategy, but a small, gender-imbalanced sample from a single school context.

title: Variability of worked examples and transfer of geometrical problem-solving skills: A cognitive-load approach
authors: Paas, F. G. W. C., & van Merriënboer, J. J. G.
design: Controlled experiment comparing four computer-based training strategies (low/high example variability crossed with worked-example vs. conventional-problem-first order)
population: Dutch secondary technical-school students learning computer numerically controlled (CNC) machinery programming
institution: University of Twente, Department of Instructional Technology, Netherlands
outcome: Students who studied high-variability worked examples invested less mental effort during practice and achieved better, less effortful transfer performance than students who practiced with low-variability examples or with conventional problem solving before worked examples.
limitations: The study used a narrow technical domain (CNC machining geometry) with a modest sample of secondary technical-school students, so results may not generalize to other subject areas, older/younger learners, or non-technical curricula.
qualityRationale: Controlled experiment with random assignment across four conditions and cognitive-load measures, but a modest sample restricted to one technical-school population and task domain.

title: A split-attention effect in multimedia learning: Evidence for dual processing systems in working memory
authors: Mayer, R. E., & Moreno, R.
design: Two randomized controlled laboratory experiments comparing narrated animation versus on-screen-text-plus-animation presentations
population: College students (Experiment 1: lightning-formation animation; Experiment 2: car braking-system animation)
institution: University of California, Santa Barbara, Department of Psychology
outcome: Students who received narration with animation (auditory + visual channels) outperformed students who received on-screen text with the same animation (visual-only, split-attention) on retention and transfer/problem-solving tests, consistent with a dual-processing (auditory/visual) working-memory model and reduced split-attention cognitive load.
limitations: The materials were short, single-session laboratory animations on lightning formation and car brakes studied by college volunteers, so findings may not directly transfer to longer, multi-session classroom multimedia instruction or younger learners.
qualityRationale: Well-controlled, randomized multi-experiment design with a relatively large combined sample (N=146) from a widely replicated foundational multimedia/cognitive-load research program.

title: Delay-retention effect with multiple-choice tests
authors: Kulhavy, R. W., & Anderson, R. C.
design: Randomized experiment with multiple immediate- and delayed-feedback conditions on an initial multiple-choice test, followed by a one-week retention retest
population: High school juniors and seniors completing a multiple-choice test on introductory psychology content
institution: Arizona State University (Kulhavy); University of Illinois (Anderson)
outcome: Delayed-feedback groups performed significantly better than immediate-feedback groups on a one-week-later retention test; the effect was attributed primarily to forgetting of interference-producing errors during the delay and secondarily to increased time spent studying the feedback after a delay.
limitations: The sample was drawn from a single population (high school students studying one introductory psychology passage), and the interference-perseveration mechanism was inferred from performance patterns rather than directly manipulated.
qualityRationale: Randomized assignment to feedback-timing conditions with a solid field sample (N=194), but single-site, pre-modern-methodology design without preregistration or multi-site replication.

title: Feedback enhances the positive effects and reduces the negative effects of multiple-choice testing
authors: Butler, A. C., & Roediger, H. L.
design: Randomized lab experiment factorially manipulating feedback (none/immediate/delayed), amount of prior study, and number of multiple-choice alternatives, followed by a one-week-later cued-recall test
population: Undergraduate psychology students
outcome: Both immediate and delayed feedback after an initial multiple-choice test increased the proportion of correct responses and reduced the proportion of intrusions from multiple-choice lures on a cued-recall test given one week later, relative to no feedback.
limitations: The authors note the to-be-learned material consisted of relatively basic factual information, and whether the feedback benefits extend to more complex conceptual material was left for future research.
qualityRationale: Tightly controlled randomized factorial lab experiment with a delayed retention test and clear mechanistic manipulation of feedback timing; a benchmark study in the testing-effect literature.

title: When Does Feedback Facilitate Learning of Words?
authors: Pashler, H., Cepeda, N. J., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D.
design: Randomized between-subjects experiment manipulating type/presence of feedback across web-based learning trials, with a final test one week later
population: Adult volunteers from an online research subject panel learning Luganda-English word pairs
venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
institution: University of California, San Diego; University of South Florida
outcome: Supplying the correct answer after an incorrect response increased one-week retention by 494% relative to no feedback, whereas feedback after correct responses produced little or no benefit for immediate or delayed performance regardless of the learner's confidence.
limitations: A reviewer noted that the Likert-type confidence scale used limited the analysis to ordinal comparisons rather than allowing cardinal calibration/absolute-accuracy evaluations.
qualityRationale: Randomized between-subjects design with a relatively large sample (N=258), a nontrivial one-week retention interval, item-level conditional analyses, and an internally replicated pattern of results.

title: Accuracy of metacognitive monitoring affects learning of texts
authors: Thiede, K. W., Anderson, M. C. M., & Therriault, D.
design: Randomized three-group lab experiment manipulating keyword-generation timing (delayed, immediate, or none) as a means of varying metacomprehension monitoring accuracy, followed by self-regulated restudy and a second test
population: Students enrolled in a psychology or educational psychology course
outcome: The delayed-keyword group showed more accurate metacomprehension monitoring than the immediate-keyword or no-keyword groups, which led to more effective self-regulated selection of texts for restudy and, in turn, higher overall test performance after restudy.
limitations: The manipulation relied on a specific keyword-generation task as a proxy for monitoring delay, and the study used a single population (University of Illinois at Chicago students) reading brief encyclopedia-style expository texts, limiting generalizability of the specific manipulation to other materials and learners.
qualityRationale: Randomized, controlled single-site lab experiment with a modest sample (N=66) directly manipulating monitoring accuracy and measuring its causal effect on self-regulated study and learning.

title: Delaying judgments of learning affects memory, not metamemory
authors: Kimball, D. R., & Metcalfe, J.
design: Three lab experiments (within- and between-subjects) manipulating judgment-of-learning (JOL) timing/format and post-JOL target reexposure during paired-associate word learning
population: Undergraduates enrolled in introductory psychology courses at Columbia University and Barnard College (36 in Experiment 1, 72 in Experiment 2, 40 in Experiment 3)
institution: Columbia University; University of Texas at Arlington
outcome: Equating spaced study opportunities via brief post-JOL reexposure eliminated the classic delayed-JOL effect (the superior accuracy of judgments of learning made after a delay), showing that the effect stems from a memory (spaced-retrieval) mechanism rather than from genuinely improved metacognitive monitoring.
limitations: The authors caution that their conclusion depends on the assumption that to-be-judged information has a similar study history at the start of the retention interval; nonequivalent study histories can make it falsely appear that JOL timing itself affects metacognitive accuracy.
qualityRationale: Three converging, tightly controlled experiments isolating a causal mechanism (spaced study vs. metacognitive monitoring) behind a well-known metacognition effect, with a combined sample of 148 participants.

title: A Region of Proximal Learning model of study time allocation
authors: Metcalfe, J., & Kornell, N.
design: Series of lab experiments (Experiment 1 reported here: within-subjects self-paced study-choice task) examining self-regulated allocation of study time based on judgments of learning and judgments of rate of learning
population: Columbia University students
outcome: When free to choose which general-knowledge items to study, participants preferentially selected items they judged as not already known (harder, unlearned items) rather than items they believed they already knew, consistent with a Region of Proximal Learning model of self-regulated study choice.
limitations: The authors explicitly note that their model describes what people do, not what they should do, and that the studies left open the question of efficacy: whether the observed self-regulation strategies actually enhance learning or are in any way optimal.
qualityRationale: Controlled lab experiment with random item assignment and clear behavioral measures, but a small single-experiment sample (N=24) drawn from one institution as part of a larger eight-experiment series.

title: Facilitating Internalization: The Self-Determination Theory Perspective
authors: Deci, E. L., Eghrari, H., Patrick, B. C., & Leone, D. R.
design: 2x2x2 factorial laboratory experiment manipulating rationale, acknowledgment of feelings, and controlling vs. autonomy-supportive language
population: Introductory psychology students fulfilling a course requirement, University of Rochester
outcome: Providing a meaningful rationale, acknowledging the person's feelings, and conveying choice (rather than control) increased subsequent free-choice engagement with a boring task, and contexts supporting self-determination produced integrated regulation (positive correlations between engagement and positive affect) while nonsupportive contexts produced introjected regulation (negative correlations).
limitations: In the nonsupportive-context subgroup only 19 subjects displayed any internalization, so correlations there did not reach conventional significance; the study also could not explain why the zero-facilitating-factor condition showed higher engagement than the one-facilitating-factor condition.
qualityRationale: Randomized factorial lab experiment with an objective behavioral measure (free-choice engagement time), but modest cell sizes (n=16-48) and a single-site convenience sample.

title: The effects of instructors' autonomy support and students' autonomous motivation on learning organic chemistry: A self-determination theory perspective
authors: Black, A. E., & Deci, E. L.
design: Prospective longitudinal field study (Time 1 / Time 2 surveys linked to objective course performance)
population: Undergraduate students enrolled in an introductory organic chemistry course at a small eastern U.S. university (137 with complete data, drawn from an initial 289)
outcome: Students' perceptions of workshop leaders' autonomy support predicted increases in autonomous self-regulation, perceived competence, and interest/enjoyment, and decreases in anxiety over the semester; leader autonomy support also predicted final course grade, especially for students who began the course low in autonomous motivation.
limitations: Autonomy support was not experimentally manipulated (correlational/prospective design), so causality cannot be firmly established; there was larger-than-optimal attrition because the Time 2 assessment was conducted unannounced and about 100 participants missed that class session.
qualityRationale: Well-controlled prospective field study with validated measures and objective exam/grade outcomes, but non-experimental (autonomy support was not manipulated) and drawn from a single course.

title: What teachers say and do to support students' autonomy during a learning activity
authors: Reeve, J., & Jang, H.
design: Laboratory experiment using a teacher-student dyad paradigm with random assignment to role; videotaped 10-minute instructional episodes coded for 20 instructional behaviors and correlated with students' perceived autonomy
population: Preservice teachers (undergraduates, 72 same-sex pairs) in a teacher certification program at a large midwestern U.S. university, randomly assigned to teacher or student role
institution: University of Iowa; University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee
outcome: Eight instructional behaviors (e.g., listening, allowing independent work, informational praise, encouragement, hints) correlated significantly and positively with students' perceived autonomy, and six controlling behaviors (e.g., monopolizing materials, uttering solutions, directives, controlling questions) correlated negatively; perceived autonomy in turn correlated positively with interest-enjoyment, engagement, and puzzle-solving performance.
limitations: Data were collected in a one-on-one laboratory setting resembling tutoring rather than a real classroom, the instructional episode lasted only 10 minutes rather than a full class period, and the teachers were inexperienced preservice teachers rather than veteran practicing teachers.
qualityRationale: Randomized experimental design (random assignment to teacher/student role), objective behavioral coding with high interrater reliability, adequate sample size, and correction for multiple comparisons (experimentwise alpha).

title: Writing About Testing Worries Boosts Exam Performance in the Classroom
authors: Ramirez, G., & Beilock, S. L.
design: Two randomized laboratory experiments plus two randomized field experiments in real high-school classrooms
population: College students (lab studies 1-2, N=20 and N=47) and ninth-grade high school biology students (field studies 3-4, N=51 and N=55), United States
institution: University of Chicago, Department of Psychology and Committee on Education
topic: anxiety, frustration and confidence in learning
outcome: A brief (10-minute) expressive-writing intervention performed immediately before a high-pressure test eliminated the 'choking under pressure' accuracy drop seen in controls, and among ninth-graders it eliminated the normally negative correlation between test anxiety and final-exam performance; highly test-anxious students who wrote about their worries outperformed highly test-anxious controls by about 6% on the final exam (B+ vs. B- average).
limitations: The classroom field experiments (studies 3 and 4) were conducted at a single school across only three biology teachers over two cohorts a year apart, limiting generalizability across institutions, teachers, and subjects.
qualityRationale: Randomized controlled design replicated across both laboratory and real classroom field experiments, with objective exam-score outcomes and within-teacher random assignment.

title: The Relationships Among Working Memory, Math Anxiety, and Performance
authors: Ashcraft, M. H., & Kirk, E. P.
design: Three-experiment study: correlational assessment of math anxiety and working-memory span (Experiment 1), a dual-task lab experiment combining mental addition with a memory-load task (Experiment 2), and a letter/number transformation working-memory task experiment (Experiment 3)
population: Undergraduate students recruited from lower-level psychology classes (66 in Experiment 1, 45 in Experiment 2, 51 in Experiment 3)
topic: anxiety, frustration and confidence in learning
outcome: Individuals with high math anxiety showed smaller computation-based working-memory spans, and this reduced capacity produced sharply higher error rates and slower responses when mental addition (especially carry problems) was performed concurrently with a memory-load task; the effect generalized to a separate, non-arithmetic letter/number transformation task.
limitations: The relation between math anxiety and performance is correlational (anxiety groups were not randomly assigned), and the authors note it becomes difficult to separate math-anxiety effects from genuine competence differences once more advanced/complex math content is tested.
qualityRationale: Well-controlled multi-experiment lab design with a dual-task manipulation and internal replication across three studies, but non-clinical convenience samples and correlational (not randomly assigned) anxiety grouping.

title: The Subtle Effects of Language Anxiety on Cognitive Processing in the Second Language
authors: MacIntyre, P. D., & Gardner, R. C.
design: Correlational study using purpose-built stage-specific anxiety scales (input, processing, output) related to nine cognitive tasks spanning the three stages of second-language acquisition
population: College students learning French as a second language, Canada
topic: anxiety, frustration and confidence in learning
outcome: Language anxiety was significantly related to performance at each of the three processing stages (input, processing, output), showing that anxiety's negative effects on second-language cognitive processing are pervasive across the learning process rather than confined to a single stage.
limitations: Correlational design using self-report anxiety scales alongside performance tasks, so the study could not establish the direction of causality between language anxiety and cognitive-processing performance.
qualityRationale: Well-designed multi-task correlational study with purpose-built stage-specific measures, but non-experimental design without random assignment or causal manipulation.

title: Schema Induction and Analogical Transfer
authors: Gick, M. L., & Holyoak, K. J.
design: Between-subjects laboratory experiment (Experiment 1 of a six-experiment paper): three conditions (analog-recall, analog-summary, control-summary) tested for spontaneous analogical transfer to Duncker's radiation/tumor convergence problem
population: High school students, grades 10-12, Bloomfield, Michigan (25 in analog-recall condition, 24 in analog-summary condition, 20 in control-summary condition)
outcome: The quality of the schema participants induced when comparing two analog stories strongly predicted successful spontaneous transfer to the analogous convergence (tumor) problem; providing a verbal or visual summary of the shared underlying principle further increased transfer rates.
limitations: The authors note their within-subject/within-condition procedure may make it difficult for a condition with a low initial noticing rate to 'catch up' in total application rate, which can bias comparisons of transfer performance across conditions.
qualityRationale: Single between-subjects lab experiment (one of six in the paper) with a modest sample (N=69); well-controlled classic design but not large-scale or preregistered.

title: The Advantage of Abstract Examples in Learning Math
authors: Kaminski, J. A., Sloutsky, V. M., & Heckler, A. F.
design: Randomized controlled laboratory experiment (Experiment 1): participants learned a novel mathematical system (a commutative group of order three) via either a single generic/abstract instantiation or one-to-three concrete instantiations, then were tested for transfer to a novel isomorphic context
population: Undergraduate college students
institution: Center for Cognitive Science, Ohio State University
outcome: Participants who learned the single generic, abstract instantiation of the mathematical concept transferred it to a novel context significantly better than participants who learned one, two, or three concrete instantiations.
limitations: The study used one simple mathematical concept (a commutative group of order three); the authors could not establish from this study alone whether the abstract-example advantage generalizes to more complex mathematical content.
qualityRationale: Randomized lab experiment with clean between-groups comparison and control over instantiation type, but modest sample (N=80) and not preregistered.

title: Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention
authors: Roediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D.
design: Two randomized laboratory experiments comparing repeated testing versus repeated restudy of prose passages, with final retention tests administered after 5 minutes, 2 days, or 1 week
population: Washington University undergraduates, ages 18-24 (Experiment 1: N=120; Experiment 2: N=180)
outcome: Repeated testing produced substantially greater retention than repeated restudying on delayed final tests (2 days and 1 week later), even though repeated restudying produced better recall on an immediate 5-minute test and increased students' confidence in their own recall.
limitations: The authors state that 'the boundary conditions for the testing effect are not yet known' and note the effect likely depends on how soon testing occurs after learning and the level of performance testing permits.
qualityRationale: Two independent, randomly-assigned, well-controlled lab experiments with a combined N=300 replicating the core effect across immediate and delayed retention intervals.

title: Retention of Spanish Vocabulary Over 8 Years
authors: Bahrick, H. P., & Phelps, E.
design: Longitudinal follow-up (delayed recall and recognition test administered 8 years after original learning/relearning of 50 English-Spanish word pairs, with original learning-session spacing varied)
population: Former college students who had originally learned Spanish-English vocabulary pairs at Ohio Wesleyan University, retested 8 years later (35 of the original 64 participants were located and retested)
venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
outcome: Retention 8 years after original learning was strongly predicted by the spacing between original learning sessions and by speed of original learning: items originally learned with a 30-day spacing interval showed about 2.5 times the recall probability of items learned with no spacing interval.
limitations: The original training conditions were modified partway through the study for most subjects (intersession intervals were changed), which the authors state 'almost certainly' diluted and underestimated the true retention differences; only 35 of the original 64 participants could be located and retested at the 8-year mark.
qualityRationale: Naturalistic longitudinal follow-up rather than a randomized experiment, with a small completer sample (N=35 of an original 64) and training conditions that were altered mid-study.

title: Models of Visuospatial and Verbal Memory Across the Adult Life Span
authors: Park, D. C., Lautenschlager, G., Hedden, T., Davidson, N. S., Smith, A. D., & Smith, P. K.
design: Large-scale cross-sectional study of short-term, working, and long-term visuospatial and verbal memory task performance across the adult lifespan, analyzed with structural/confirmatory factor models
population: Community-dwelling adults spanning the adult life span (20s to 90s)
institution: Department of Psychology, University of Michigan (with co-authors at University of Georgia and Georgia Institute of Technology)
outcome: Beginning in the 20s, a continuous, regular decline occurred with age on processing-intensive tasks (speed of processing, working memory, long-term memory), whereas verbal knowledge increased across the life span; visuospatial and verbal working memory were distinct but highly interrelated systems, with little behavioral evidence of dedifferentiation of function in older compared with younger adults.
limitations: The design is cross-sectional rather than longitudinal, so age-related differences may be confounded with cohort effects rather than reflecting true within-person developmental change.
qualityRationale: Large sample (N=345) with rigorous structural modeling, but a correlational/quasi-experimental cross-sectional design since age cannot be randomly assigned.

title: Further Testing of Limits of Cognitive Plasticity: Negative Age Differences in a Mnemonic Skill Are Robust
authors: Baltes, P. B., & Kliegl, R.
design: Testing-the-limits training study: quasi-experimental age-group comparison with extensive within-subject practice (38 training sessions) on the method-of-loci mnemonic skill for serial word-list recall
population: 16 young adults (ages 20-30) and 19 older adults (ages 66-80) in Berlin, Germany
institution: Max Planck Institute for Human Development and Education, Berlin, Germany
outcome: Even after 38 sessions of training on the method of loci, older adults' memory performance remained below that of younger adults after only two initial instructional sessions, with no meaningful overlap between the age groups, indicating a robust age-related ceiling on learning gains from extended practice on this mnemonic skill.
limitations: The authors caution the finding is specific to this particular mnemonic component of fluid-intelligence-related performance and should not be generalized to all cognitive domains; they also note the ceiling finding 'is never final in an absolute sense,' since further practice or different response formats might yield different results.
qualityRationale: Small, tightly controlled quasi-experimental age-group comparison (N=35) with extensive within-subject training; not randomized since age is an inherent subject variable.

title: Repeated Testing Produces Superior Transfer of Learning Relative to Repeated Studying
authors: Butler, A. C.
design: Four within-subjects lab experiments. Subjects studied prose passages, then either repeatedly restudied passages or repeatedly took cued-recall tests on them; one week later a final test assessed either retention of the same questions (Exp 1a), transfer to new inferential questions from the same knowledge domain (Exp 1b, 2), or transfer to new inferential questions from a different knowledge domain (Exp 3).
population: Undergraduate psychology students at Washington University in St. Louis (24 in Experiment 1a, 24 in Experiment 1b; separate independent undergraduate samples completed Experiments 2 and 3), participating for course credit or pay.
venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
outcome: Repeated testing produced superior retention and transfer relative to repeated studying across all four experiments; e.g., in Experiment 1a, factual same-test performance was .76 vs. restudy .27, t(23) = 9.97, d = 2.13, and variable-test performance was .75 vs. .27, t(23) = 10.40, d = 2.09. Benefits held even when final-test questions required new inferential answers from a different knowledge domain (Experiment 3).
limitations: All-undergraduate, single-institution samples across experiments; the author notes at least one planned comparison (control-question effect in Experiment 1b) failed to reach significance 'likely due to insufficient power,' and the hypothesized encoding-variability mechanism (rephrased vs. same test questions) was not supported, limiting mechanistic conclusions.
qualityRationale: Four well-controlled within-subjects lab experiments with random assignment to condition and large, clearly reported effect sizes; undergraduate convenience samples at one university, not preregistered.

title: The Effects of Overlearning and Distributed Practice on the Retention of Mathematics Knowledge
authors: Rohrer, D., & Taylor, K.
design: Two lab experiments in which college students learned a mathematical procedure (permutation problems) and then practiced 10 problems either massed in a single session or distributed across two sessions one week apart, with an additional overlearning condition (6 extra massed problems); retention was tested either 1 or 4 weeks later.
population: College students learning to solve mathematics (permutation) problems, combined across two experiments.
outcome: Distributing the 10 practice problems across two sessions one week apart nearly doubled performance on the 4-week retention test relative to massing them in one session; the distributed-practice benefit was negligible at 1 week but very large at 4 weeks. The additional overlearning problems had no effect on test scores at either retention interval.
limitations: College-student sample learning a single narrow mathematical procedure in a lab-like (non-classroom) setting; only two spacing gaps and two retention intervals were tested, so the full shape of the spacing-retention relationship was not established.
qualityRationale: Controlled two-experiment lab study with random assignment to spacing/overlearning conditions and a clear dissociation of effects; single-institution college-student convenience sample, not preregistered.

title: Spacing Effects in Real-World Classroom Vocabulary Learning
authors: Sobel, H. S., Cepeda, N. J., & Kapler, I. V.
design: Within-subjects classroom field experiment. Each child learned 4 GRE-level English vocabulary words in a massed condition (two learning sessions separated by under 1 minute) and 4 different words in a spaced condition (two sessions separated by 1 week), taught by the regular classroom teacher; definition recall was tested 5 weeks after the second learning session for each condition.
population: Fifth-grade children (mean age approximately 10 years; 19 female) from two classrooms in an upper-middle-SES Ontario, Canada middle school (46 recruited; 7 dropped for missing sessions).
outcome: Percentage of definitions recalled at the 5-week final test was 177% higher in the spaced condition (M = 20.8%, SEM = 4.3) than the massed condition (M = 7.5%, SEM = 2.0), paired t(38) = 3.0, p = .004, d = 0.48.
limitations: Small sample drawn from just two classrooms in a single school; only one spacing interval (1 week) and one retention interval (5 weeks) were tested; only vocabulary material was examined, so the authors note generalization to math or science content remains untested.
qualityRationale: Real-world classroom field experiment with a within-subjects design and an objective, blind-scored outcome measure; small single-school sample (n=39) over a single cohort, not preregistered or multi-site.

title: The Benefit of Interleaved Mathematics Practice Is Not Limited to Superficially Similar Kinds of Problems
authors: Rohrer, D., Dedrick, R. F., & Burgess, K.
design: Classroom-based, counterbalanced crossover field experiment. Seventh-grade students received blocked or interleaved mathematics practice, using problem kinds that were superficially dissimilar from each other (unlike earlier interleaving studies), delivered by their regular teacher within their regular course over a nine-week period; students sat an unannounced test two weeks after the final practice assignment.
population: Grade 7 mathematics students in a regular classroom setting.
institution: University of South Florida, Tampa, FL
outcome: Mean test scores were greater for material learned via interleaved practice than blocked practice (72% vs. 38%), d = 1.05, even though the different kinds of problems were superficially dissimilar, showing the interleaving benefit is not limited to problems that look alike.
limitations: Single set of classrooms and one regular teacher's implementation over one nine-week period, limiting generalization across teachers, schools, and math topics; a quasi-experimental classroom crossover design rather than individually randomized lab control.
qualityRationale: Real classroom field experiment (n=140, grade 7) with a counterbalanced crossover design, delivered by regular teachers, and a delayed unannounced test; single-school implementation, not preregistered or multi-site, so graded B despite strong ecological validity.

title: Evaluation of Children's Cognitive Load in Processing and Storage of Their Spatial Working Memory
authors: Chen, H.-C., Kao, C.-H., Wang, T.-H., & Lai, Y.-T.
design: Two lab experiments using a spatial complex-span task; processing-task complexity (high vs. low) manipulated between subjects and memory set size (2 vs. 3) manipulated within subjects, with cognitive load assessed via task accuracy, self-report ratings, and pupil dilation (eye-tracking).
population: Taiwanese 11-year-old elementary school children from two public elementary schools in urban northern Taiwan (Experiment 1: N=80; Experiment 2: N=72, split into high-complexity n=34 and low-complexity n=38 groups).
institution: National Tsing Hua University (Dept. of Early Childhood Education; Dept. of Education and Learning Technology) and National Taiwan University Hsin-Chu Hospital, Taiwan
outcome: Memory-task accuracy was significantly lower under high-complexity processing (M=0.73) than low-complexity processing (M=0.83); self-reported effort for the memory task increased with larger set sizes; stepwise regression showed subjective difficulty ratings predicted memory performance in low-complexity conditions, while pupil dilation during processing predicted performance in high-complexity conditions.
limitations: Authors note the immediate (concurrent) cognitive-load ratings could distract children from the ongoing task and interfere with working-memory operation itself; the between-subjects complexity manipulation limited within-child comparison, and pupil-dilation results showed inconsistent patterns, possibly due to small set sizes.
qualityRationale: Controlled quasi-experimental lab study across two samples (N=80, N=72) with multi-method (behavioral, self-report, physiological) measurement; single-site, not preregistered, so graded as a solid controlled experiment rather than an A-tier RCT/multisite synthesis.

title: The Effect of Type and Timing of Feedback on Learning From Multiple-Choice Tests
authors: Butler, A. C., Karpicke, J. D., & Roediger, H. L., III
design: Two experiments: participants read prose passages, took an initial six-alternative multiple-choice test with feedback timing (immediate vs. delayed) and feedback type (standard vs. answer-until-correct) manipulated factorially, then completed a delayed cued-recall test assessing long-term retention.
population: Washington University in St. Louis undergraduates participating for course credit or payment (Experiment 1: N=48; Experiment 2: N=40).
outcome: Delayed feedback produced superior final cued-recall performance relative to immediate feedback, with the advantage larger in Experiment 2 (1-week retention interval) than Experiment 1 (1-day interval); feedback type (standard vs. answer-until-correct) did not significantly affect learning in either experiment.
limitations: Authors note that in applied classroom settings students may not fully process delayed feedback unless required to, whereas the lab procedure enforced feedback processing for a fixed duration regardless of correctness — a condition unlikely to hold under normal classroom review, and the tested retention intervals (1 day, 1 week) leave open whether the delayed-feedback benefit persists at longer delays.
qualityRationale: Two-experiment lab replication with a full factorial mixed design and direct replication of the core effect across experiments, but a single-institution convenience sample and no preregistration, so graded as a controlled experiment rather than A-tier.

title: Achievement Goals Affect Metacognitive Judgments
authors: Ikeda, K., Yue, C. L., Murayama, K., & Castel, A. D.
design: Five experiments manipulating achievement-goal instructions (mastery-approach vs. performance-approach) before a paired-associate word-list memory task, measuring judgments of learning (JOLs) and subsequent cued-recall accuracy, synthesized with an internal meta-analysis across experiments.
population: Mixed adult samples recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk (Experiments 1a N=86, 1b N=53, 2a N=77, 2b N=237) and undergraduate students (Experiment 3, N=78).
institution: Nagoya University; University of Reading; Kochi University of Technology; Covenant College; University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)
outcome: Performance-approach goal framing produced significantly higher metacognitive judgments (JOLs) than mastery-approach framing (d = 0.44, 95% CI [0.24, 0.63]) despite negligible differences in actual recall performance (d = 0.07, 95% CI [-0.12, 0.27]), indicating achievement-goal framing biases metacognitive monitoring independent of actual learning outcomes.
limitations: Authors state the precise mechanism behind the goal-induced inflation of metacognitive judgments is unclear; most samples were online MTurk workers doing a decontextualized memory task rather than students pursuing authentic academic goals, limiting generalization to real classroom self-regulation.
qualityRationale: Five internally-replicated experiments (total N=531) across multiple labs with a meta-analytic synthesis of effect sizes, but not a coordinated preregistered multisite RCT, so graded as a strong controlled-experiment replication rather than A-tier.

title: Motivating Learning, Performance, and Persistence: The Synergistic Effects of Intrinsic Goal Contents and Autonomy-Supportive Contexts
authors: Vansteenkiste, M., Simons, J., Lens, W., Sheldon, K. M., & Deci, E. L.
design: Three field experiments embedded in real classes using a 2 (intrinsic vs. extrinsic goal framing) x 2 (autonomy-supportive vs. controlling instructional style) factorial design, testing effects on depth of processing, conceptual test performance, and free-choice persistence, with autonomous motivation tested as a mediator.
population: Study 1: 200 first-year female Belgian college students (19-20 years old) training to become preschool teachers, tested during regular university classes in Belgium learning text material on recycling; Studies 2 and 3 replicated the design with Belgian marketing/business-communication college students and with high-school students learning Tai-bo exercise routines.
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
institution: University of Leuven (Belgium); University of Missouri-Columbia; University of Rochester
outcome: In Study 1, intrinsic (vs. extrinsic) goal framing and autonomy-supportive (vs. controlling) instructional style each produced significant main effects on depth of processing, test performance, and free-choice persistence; the goal-framing x autonomy-support interaction was significant on 4 of 5 outcome variables, and participants' autonomous motivation significantly mediated these effects (mediated variance ranged 23%-52% across outcomes); Studies 2 and 3 replicated and extended this pattern to new populations and content.
limitations: Sample restricted to Belgian students in structured intact-classroom settings, all-female in Study 1, using brief single-session learning tasks, so generalization to sustained real-world motivation and other cultures is untested; the persistence outcome relied on a brief free-choice behavioral measure rather than long-term engagement.
qualityRationale: Three-experiment field-replication design with random assignment within intact classes and mediation analysis, strong internal validity but single-country convenience samples and no preregistration, so graded as a controlled experiment rather than A-tier.

title: Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety
authors: Horwitz, E. K., Horwitz, M. B., & Cope, J. A.
design: Theory-building empirical study combining clinical observation of foreign language learners with development and preliminary psychometric validation of the Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety Scale (FLCAS), a 33-item Likert self-report instrument assessing communication apprehension, test anxiety, and fear of negative evaluation specific to foreign language classrooms.
population: University students at the University of Texas at Austin enrolled in foreign language courses; the construct was developed from the authors' clinical experience teaching foreign language students plus direct feedback from 30 students attending a university support group for foreign-language-learning anxiety, with the resulting scale then administered to an introductory foreign language class.
topic: anxiety, frustration and confidence in learning
outcome: Introduced the FLCAS (33 items; reported internal consistency alpha = .93, test-retest reliability r = .83) and established foreign language anxiety as a situation-specific anxiety construct distinct from general trait anxiety, arising because foreign language performance uniquely threatens self-concept and self-expression.
limitations: The theory and initial construct evolved largely from clinical/anecdotal observation and a small, non-random support-group sample (N=30) rather than a large probability sample; later factor-analytic work (e.g., Aida, 1994) questioned whether the scale's proposed subcomponents hold up, and other researchers (Sparks & Ganschow) challenged whether the FLCAS measures anxiety per se or underlying language-skill deficits.
qualityRationale: Foundational field study combining clinical/qualitative observation with a newly developed and psychometrically tested self-report scale; the initial development sample was small and non-random rather than an RCT, but it is the seminal primary empirical source for the construct and its scale has since been extremely widely replicated and validated.

title: Learning and Transfer: A General Role for Analogical Encoding
authors: Gentner, D., Loewenstein, J., & Thompson, L.
design: Three between-subjects lab experiments manipulating whether novice negotiators compared two analogous training cases (analogical encoding), studied the same two cases separately, or received no training, then measured transfer of the embedded negotiation principle (trade-off or contingent contract) to a novel written test case (Experiments 1-2) or an actual face-to-face negotiation (Experiment 3).
population: Undergraduate students at Northwestern University participating to fulfill a course requirement (Experiment 1: N=48; Experiment 2: N=128; Experiment 3: N=158, negotiating in 79 pairs plus baseline).
institution: Northwestern University (Department of Psychology and Kellogg School of Management)
outcome: Comparing two analogous cases produced far greater transfer than studying cases separately or no training: in Experiment 2, 48% of comparison-condition participants transferred the trained principle to a novel case versus 19% of separate-cases participants (chi-square(1, N=128)=11.85, p<.01); in Experiment 3's live negotiation, 90% of guided-analogy pairs and 70% of comparison pairs formed the target agreement versus 55% (separate cases) and 37% (baseline, no training).
limitations: Participants were novice undergraduate negotiators in a single domain (negotiation) using relatively short, single-session lab or paper-and-pencil tasks; the authors note that most of their supporting evidence, including this study, comes from a narrow population (college undergraduates), leaving open how the effect generalizes to more expert learners or less scaffolded real-world settings.
qualityRationale: Three converging, adequately powered, randomized between-subjects lab experiments (combined N=334) with blind coding (86-93% inter-rater agreement) culminating in a real behavioral transfer outcome (live face-to-face negotiation) in Experiment 3, going beyond a single small quasi-experiment.

title: Interdomain Transfer Between Isomorphic Topics in Algebra and Physics
authors: Bassok, M., & Holyoak, K. J.
design: Three experiments testing spontaneous transfer of a learned mathematical procedure between structurally isomorphic subtopics of algebra (arithmetic-progression word problems) and physics (constant-acceleration word problems); Experiment 1 used individual instruction with think-aloud verbal protocols and a within-subject pretest/posttest/transfer-test design comparing algebra-trained versus physics-trained groups.
population: Experiment 1: 12 ninth-grade high-ability students (5 male, 7 female) from an accelerated science program in a public high school in Pittsburgh, who had not previously studied either arithmetic progressions or constant acceleration; Experiments 2 and 3 extended testing to further high school and college student samples.
venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
institution: University of Pittsburgh (Learning Research and Development Center) and University of California, Los Angeles
outcome: Transfer was highly asymmetric: students trained on arithmetic-progression algebra applied the learned method to physics problems on 72% of transfer trials, whereas students trained on constant-acceleration physics applied the learned method to algebra problems on only 10% of transfer trials (interaction F(1,10)=25.3, p<.001); verbal protocols showed the algebra-to-physics recognition was immediate and content-free.
limitations: Experiment 1's core sample was very small (N=12) and drawn from an academically selected accelerated-program group, limiting generalizability; the asymmetric-transfer effect required subjects to have well-learned, abstractly encoded source-domain procedures, which the authors note is not typical of how most classroom content is actually taught.
qualityRationale: Controlled multi-experiment lab study with random assignment to training condition and detailed verbal-protocol analysis, but the reported core experiment used a small, non-representative sample (N=12), making it a rigorous but small-scale quasi-experimental design rather than an A-grade large or preregistered study.

title: Semantic Memory Content in Permastore: Fifty Years of Memory for Spanish Learned in School
authors: Bahrick, H. P.
design: Cross-sectional retention study testing recognition, free recall, and reading comprehension of Spanish vocabulary, idioms, and grammar learned in school, combined with a questionnaire on original degree of training (courses taken, grades) and amount of rehearsal since training, across retention intervals of 0-50 years.
population: Adults who had studied Spanish in school or college between 1 and 50 years prior to testing, varying widely in original degree of learning and in subsequent rehearsal/use of Spanish.
outcome: Content originally learned to a high degree showed rapid decline for roughly the first 3-6 years, followed by a long 'permastore' plateau of stable retention lasting up to 50 years with little further measurable loss, whereas content learned to a low original degree decayed toward floor levels much earlier.
limitations: Cross-sectional (not longitudinal) design conflates cohort differences with true retention-interval effects; the sample was self-selected from alumni reachable decades later, and original degree of learning was reconstructed retrospectively via self-report and school records rather than experimentally controlled at the time of acquisition.
qualityRationale: Large-sample (N=733) systematic field study with multiple converging memory measures spanning five decades, but it is a non-randomized, retrospective, cross-sectional design rather than a true longitudinal or experimental study.

title: Fifty Years of Memory for Names and Faces: A Cross-Sectional Approach
authors: Bahrick, H. P., Bahrick, P. O., & Wittlinger, R. P.
design: Cross-sectional study testing recognition and free recall of former high school classmates' names and yearbook photographs, sampling different cohorts of graduates to cover retention intervals ranging from 2 weeks to 57 years since graduation.
population: High school graduates tested for memory of classmates selected from their own yearbooks, sampled across cohorts spanning nearly six decades since graduation.
outcome: Recognition accuracy for names and faces remained around the 90% level for up to about 35 years post-graduation before declining to roughly 75% by 48 years, while free recall of names showed a much earlier and steeper decline than recognition or photo-matching measures.
limitations: Cross-sectional design cannot fully separate true forgetting curves from cohort and self-selection effects (e.g., differential availability of old yearbooks or willingness of older alumni to participate); the study relies on retrospective identification of decades-old acquaintances rather than controlled learning of new material.
qualityRationale: Large-sample (N=392), methodologically careful cross-sectional field study spanning nearly six decades of retention interval with multiple converging measures (recognition, matching, free recall), but it is not a randomized or longitudinal experimental design.

title: On the Very Long-Term Retention of Knowledge Acquired Through Formal Education: Twelve Years of Cognitive Psychology
authors: Conway, M. A., Cohen, G., & Stanhope, N.
design: Cross-sectional retention study testing former students' recognition and cued recall of researcher names, concepts, and conceptual relations taught in an undergraduate cognitive psychology course, sampling different cohorts who had taken the course between 1978 and 1989 to cover retention intervals up to 12 years.
population: Former undergraduate students who had taken a formal cognitive psychology course at a UK university between 1978 and 1989, tested at varying intervals of up to 12 years after completing the course.
outcome: Memory for proper names of researchers and for specific concepts/conceptual relations declined substantially over roughly the first 3 years after the course and then stabilized at an above-chance plateau for up to 12 years, whereas memory for general facts and research methods remained comparatively stable across the entire retention period.
limitations: Cross-sectional sampling of different cohorts at a single testing point conflates individual/cohort differences with true retention-interval effects; original degree of learning (grades, engagement) was not experimentally controlled, and self-selection of alumni willing to be retested may bias the sample toward more engaged former students.
qualityRationale: Large-sample (N=373) systematic field study of real classroom-based learning tracked over up to 12 years, but it is a cross-sectional/quasi-experimental design rather than a randomized or fully within-subject longitudinal study.

title: Optimizing Schedules of Retrieval Practice for Durable and Efficient Learning: How Much Is Enough?
authors: Rawson, K. A., & Dunlosky, J.
design: Three lab experiments crossing initial-learning criterion (1, 2, 3, or 4 correct recalls in an initial session) with number of subsequent relearning sessions (1-5), each relearned to one correct recall, followed by a delayed criterial test.
population: 533 undergraduate students who learned concept definitions via computerized retrieval practice with restudy across the three experiments.
outcome: Durable, efficient long-term retention was best achieved by an initial learning criterion of 3 correct recalls followed by relearning to 1 correct recall in 3 additional widely spaced sessions; prior literature had not combined initial-criterion and relearning-schedule manipulations.
limitations: Single content domain (declarative concept definitions) studied by college students in a computer-administered lab paradigm; unclear whether the optimal criterion-by-relearning combination generalizes to other material types, real classroom conditions, or non-college populations.
qualityRationale: Controlled, randomized multi-experiment lab study with a large single-site sample and extensive item-level scoring, but single institution, single material domain, and not preregistered or multisite.

title: Examining Age Differences in Performance of a Complex Information Search and Retrieval Task
authors: Czaja, S. J., Sharit, J., Ownby, R., Roth, D. L., & Nair, S.
design: Cross-sectional lab study in which participants performed a simulated health-insurance customer-service information search and retrieval task across 3 days, with cognitive ability testing and analysis of task-experience effects.
population: 117 community-based adults across three age cohorts: younger (20-39 years), middle-aged (40-59 years), and older (60-75 years).
institution: University of Miami; Johns Hopkins University
outcome: Significant age-related differences were found on most task-performance measures (with the exception of navigational efficiency and correct problems navigated per attempt); task experience improved performance over the 3 days, and component cognitive abilities (e.g., working memory, spatial ability) showed both direct and indirect relations to task performance.
limitations: Simulated rather than real on-the-job task; cross-sectional design confounds age with birth cohort; sample was a community-based volunteer group whose generalizability to all complex real-world information-search tasks is uncertain.
qualityRationale: Controlled lab-based quasi-experiment with a life-span age-group comparison and multi-day repeated task performance, but cross-sectional, single simulated task, and single research center.

title: Decomposing Adult Age Differences in Working Memory
authors: Salthouse, T. A., & Babcock, R. L.
design: Two cross-sectional lab studies administering multiple working-memory tasks alongside measures of storage capacity, processing efficiency, coordination effectiveness, and simple comparison speed, then statistically partialing these components out of age-working memory correlations.
population: 460 adults aged 18 to 87 across the two studies (Study 1 included 227 participants completing eight tasks).
institution: Georgia Institute of Technology, School of Psychology
outcome: Age correlated negatively with working-memory measures (r = -.39 to -.52); these age-working memory relations were substantially attenuated after partialing out simple processing-speed measures, more so than storage-capacity, processing-efficiency, or coordination measures, implicating processing speed as a major mediator of age-related working-memory decline.
limitations: Cross-sectional (not longitudinal) design confounds age with cohort effects, and the correlational partialing approach cannot establish that processing speed causally drives working-memory decline rather than merely covarying with it.
qualityRationale: Large single-site cross-sectional lab study spanning a wide adult age range with multiple converging tasks, but correlational/cross-sectional design rather than a preregistered or multisite RCT.

title: Cultivating Competence, Self-Efficacy, and Intrinsic Interest Through Proximal Self-Motivation
authors: Bandura, A., & Schunk, D. H.
design: Randomized controlled experiment: children with diagnosed arithmetic deficits engaged in self-paced, self-directed subtraction learning over seven 30-min sessions under one of three treatment conditions (proximal subgoals, distal goals, or suggestion to work without goals) or a no-treatment control; self-efficacy and subtraction performance assessed pre- and post-treatment via analysis of variance and Newman-Keuls comparisons.
population: 40 children (21 boys, 19 girls) ages 7.3-10.1 years (M=8.4), predominantly middle-class, drawn from six elementary schools in the Palo Alto Unified School District after teacher referral for gross deficits and low interest in arithmetic.
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
outcome: Significant main effect of treatment on self-efficacy, F(3,36)=10.13, p<.001, and a treatment x phase interaction, F(6,72)=5.96, p<.001; children in the proximal-subgoal condition showed rapid self-directed progress, substantial mastery of subtraction operations, and increased self-efficacy and intrinsic interest, while distal goals produced no demonstrable benefit over the no-goal or control conditions.
limitations: Very small per-condition cell sizes (~10 children per group) drawn from a narrow, clinically-referred sample with pre-existing arithmetic deficits at a single school district, limiting statistical power and generalizability to typically-achieving learners or non-mathematical domains.
qualityRationale: True randomized experiment with objective performance measures, but small single-site sample with a clinically-selected population limits power and external validity relative to an A-grade multisite/preregistered study.

title: Goals and Progress Feedback: Effects on Self-Efficacy and Writing Achievement
authors: Schunk, D. H., & Swartz, C. W.
design: Two classroom experiments manipulating goal type (process/learning goal vs. general 'do your best' goal vs. no goal) crossed with progress feedback on paragraph-writing strategy instruction; self-efficacy and writing skill measured pre-, mid-, and post-instruction plus maintenance and generalization follow-up tests.
population: 100 upper-elementary students of average writing ability across two experiments: 60 fifth graders (Experiment 1) and 40 fourth graders (Experiment 2) from public elementary schools.
institution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
outcome: The process (learning) goal combined with progress feedback produced the greatest gains in self-efficacy and writing achievement, and self-efficacy was highly predictive of subsequent writing skill and strategy use; effects held up at maintenance and generalization testing.
limitations: Sample restricted to upper-elementary students in a single writing domain (paragraph composition) and short-term instructional intervention, limiting evidence about durability and transfer to other academic domains.
qualityRationale: Controlled classroom experiment with two internal replications and direct manipulation of both goal type and progress feedback, but modest sample sizes and a single school setting keep it below an A-grade preregistered/multisite design.

title: Improving Job Performance Through Training in Goal Setting
authors: Latham, G. P., & Kinne, S. B.
design: Field experiment: logging crews/operators were matched and randomly assigned to a 1-day training program in specific goal setting or a no-training control condition; production, employee turnover, absenteeism, and injuries were recorded for 12 consecutive weeks and analyzed via analysis of variance.
population: 20 pulpwood-logging operators/crews employed in an industrial logging operation in the Pacific Northwest.
institution: Weyerhaeuser Company (with Gary P. Latham affiliated with the University of Washington)
outcome: Goal-setting training significantly increased production and significantly decreased absenteeism in the trained group relative to the untrained control group over the 12-week field period.
limitations: Very small unit-level sample (20 crews/operators) from a single company and industry, with brief 12-week follow-up, limiting statistical power and generalizability beyond manual logging work.
qualityRationale: Genuine field experiment with matched random assignment to real job conditions, but a very small N of organizational units and single-company scope place it below A-grade multisite/preregistered evidence.

title: Examining the Effects of Goal-Setting, Feedback, and Incentives on Sustained Attention
authors: Robison, M. K., Unsworth, N., & Brewer, G. A.
design: Preregistered four-experiment, a priori power-analyzed, between-subjects lab study. Experiment 1 (used here) randomly assigned participants to a no-goal, easy-specific-goal, or hard/difficult-specific-goal condition on a 30-minute psychomotor vigilance task; Experiment 2 crossed goal-setting with trial/block-level progress feedback; outcomes (reaction time, vigilance decrement, task-unrelated thoughts, motivation, alertness) were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models and Bayes Factors.
population: 105 undergraduate students from the University of Oregon human subjects pool (104 analyzed after 1 exclusion; 74 women, 30 men; Mage=19.16, SD=1.93), completing the task for partial course credit.
venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
institution: University of Texas at Arlington; University of Oregon; Arizona State University
outcome: Specific goals (both easy and hard) reduced reaction times and attenuated the vigilance decrement relative to vague/no-goal instructions in Experiment 1; in Experiment 2, combining a specific goal with progress feedback produced markedly stronger effects on both task performance and task engagement, and feedback alone increased motivation and reduced task-unrelated thoughts regardless of goal condition.
limitations: Authors report that none of the manipulations, including goal+feedback, fully eliminated the vigilance decrement; incentives (Experiment 3) did not improve performance and a moderately-difficult goal (Experiment 4) showed no added benefit, and the sample was limited to university undergraduates on a single simple reaction-time task.
qualityRationale: Preregistered, a priori sample-size-determined, multi-experiment design directly manipulating goal specificity/difficulty and progress feedback with Bayesian and mixed-effects confirmatory analysis, meeting the bar for large/preregistered controlled experimental evidence.

title: How Are Habits Formed: Modelling Habit Formation in the Real World
authors: Lally, P., van Jaarsveld, C. H. M., Potts, H. W. W., & Wardle, J.
design: Longitudinal diary field study: participants selected a daily eating, drinking, or activity behaviour to perform in a stable context (e.g., 'after breakfast') for 12 weeks (84 days), completing a daily online Self-Report Habit Index measuring automaticity; nonlinear curve-fitting modelled growth of automaticity across repetitions at the individual level.
population: Adult volunteers (staff, students, and family/friends recruited by a UK university research team), mostly postgraduate students, mean age approximately 27; 82 completed the 12-week study.
institution: University College London (Department of Epidemiology and Public Health / Behavioural Science and Health), London, UK
outcome: Automaticity increased following an asymptotic (not linear) curve; among the 39 of 82 completers whose data fit the model adequately, median time to reach 95% of maximum automaticity was 66 days (range 18-254 days); exercise habits took longer (median 91 days) than eating/drinking habits (59-65 days); missing single opportunities to perform the behaviour did not materially disrupt habit formation.
limitations: Only 39 of 82 completing participants (48%) produced curve fits with adequate model fit, so the headline timeline estimates rest on fewer than half the original sample, and the self-selected volunteer sample chose their own moderately easy health behaviours rather than being randomly assigned one.
qualityRationale: Naturalistic observational diary field study with no control group or random assignment; strength comes from individual-level growth-curve modelling of real repeated behaviour over 12 weeks rather than experimental manipulation.

title: Changing Circumstances, Disrupting Habits
authors: Wood, W., Tam, L., & Guerrero Witt, M.
design: Two-wave longitudinal field study surveying university transfer students one month before and one month after relocating, measuring self-reported frequency of three daily behaviours (exercising, newspaper reading, TV watching), intentions, and performance-context stability (location, co-participants, timing) to test whether context change disrupts cue-triggered habits.
population: College students transferring to Texas A&M University.
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
institution: Duke University and Texas A&M University
outcome: Habits (exercising, newspaper reading, TV watching) persisted after the campus transfer only when the performance context stayed the same (e.g., continuing to read the paper with the same companions); when context cues changed, habitual performance was disrupted and behaviour came back under the control of participants' current intentions -- described by the authors as the first study demonstrating everyday behaviour change through an unplanned change in performance context.
limitations: Relies on self-report behaviour frequency and retrospective context ratings collected at only two survey waves one month apart, and is limited to a single naturalistic transition event (university transfer) rather than an experimentally controlled manipulation of context.
qualityRationale: Naturalistic two-wave longitudinal field study exploiting a real-life context change (university transfer) rather than a randomized experiment; causal claims about cue/context disruption rely on comparing stable- vs. changed-context habits rather than random assignment.

title: App-Based Habit Building Reduces Motivational Impairments During Studying: An Event Sampling Study
authors: Stojanovic, M., Grund, A., & Fries, S.
design: Event-sampling field study: participants used a smartphone app to log daily study-habit repetitions over 6 weeks, rating automaticity (Self-Report Behavioral Automaticity Index items), want/should conflict, and motivational interference after each logged repetition; multilevel modelling tested growth of automaticity with cumulative repetitions and its downstream motivational effects.
population: Undergraduate psychology students (79.1% female, mean age 22.3) at two German universities, all iPhone users, earning course credit.
institution: Bielefeld University, Department of Psychology, Germany
outcome: Automaticity increased with habit repetitions along an asymptotic curve (replicating Lally et al.), from 2,574 total logged repetitions (M = 28.29 per person); want-should conflict decreased as automaticity increased (b = -0.200, p < .001) and motivational interference decreased with automaticity (b = -0.100, p < .001); trait self-control's effect on studying was fully mediated by general study-habit strength; average self-reported goal attainment across repetitions was 83.4%.
limitations: Sample restricted to young, predominantly female, German psychology students earning course credit, which the authors note limits generalizability; the in-situ event-sampling design and credit incentive may have produced artificial compliance, and general study-habit strength was used only as a proxy rather than a full behavioural composition analysis.
qualityRationale: Naturalistic event-sampling/diary field study with a homogeneous convenience sample, course-credit incentive, and no random assignment or control condition, though it directly replicates and extends automaticity growth-curve findings using real repeated study behaviour relevant to learning-app return behaviour.
