title: Habit Formation Following Routine-Based Versus Time-Based Cue Planning: A Randomized Controlled Trial
authors: Keller, J., Kwasnicka, D., Klaiber, P., Sichert, L., Lally, P., & Fleig, L.
design: Randomized controlled trial: participants were randomly assigned to link a new daily nutrition behaviour to either a routine-based cue or a time-based cue, then completed daily diary measures of automaticity (Self-Report Behavioral Automaticity Index) and plan enactment for 84 days; multilevel growth modelling estimated automaticity trajectories and predictors of peak automaticity.
population: Adults aged 18-77 recruited for a nutrition habit-formation intervention.
institution: Freie Universitat Berlin, MSB Medical School Berlin, University College London, University of British Columbia, and University of Melbourne / SWPS University of Social Sciences and Humanities (multi-site author collaboration)
outcome: Both routine-based and time-based cue planning were similarly effective for habit formation, with no significant between-group difference in automaticity growth; among participants who successfully formed a habit, median time to reach peak automaticity was 59 days; repeated plan enactment (actually performing the planned behaviour in response to the cue) was the key predictor of automaticity gains, more so than the type of cue used.
limitations: Self-selected volunteer sample recruited specifically for a nutrition-behaviour trial, reliance on self-report daily diary measures of automaticity and plan adherence over 84 days, and only a subset of participants reached a stable automaticity asymptote from which the median day-59 estimate was derived.
qualityRationale: Randomized controlled trial with random assignment to routine-based vs. time-based cue-planning conditions, daily diary tracking over 12 weeks, and multilevel growth-curve modelling -- the strongest design in this set for causal inference about cue-based habit-formation mechanisms.

title: The Effect of Overlearning on Long-Term Retention
authors: Rohrer, D., Taylor, K., Pashler, H., Wixted, J. T., & Cepeda, N. J.
design: Two between-subjects laboratory experiments manipulating initial learning level (Low vs. High, via 5 vs. 20 test-with-feedback trials with equal total study time) crossed with retention interval (Experiment 1: 1, 3, or 9 weeks; Experiment 2: 1 or 4 weeks); Experiment 1 used city-country paired associates, Experiment 2 used word-definition pairs.
population: College undergraduates at the University of South Florida (130 enrolled/122 analyzed in Experiment 1; 88 enrolled/75 analyzed in Experiment 2).
outcome: Overlearners (Hi condition) recalled far more than Low learners at the 1-week test, but this advantage decreased dramatically thereafter and had disappeared by the 9-week test in Experiment 1 and the 4-week test in Experiment 2; higher learners forgot at proportionally greater rates than lower learners.
limitations: Authors state results may not generalize beyond paired-associate verbal tasks and note uncertainty about whether the shrinking-benefit pattern holds for abstract skills such as mathematical procedures or for free-recall/recognition outcome measures.
qualityRationale: Two independent, controlled lab experiments with random assignment to learning level, manipulated retention interval, equal study time across conditions, and a reasonably large combined sample (N=218); main limitation is restriction to paired-associate verbal materials.

title: Mastery Learning of Advanced Cardiac Life Support Skills by Internal Medicine Residents Using Simulation Technology and Deliberate Practice
authors: Wayne, D. B., Butter, J., Siddall, V. J., Fudala, M. J., Wade, L. D., Feinglass, J., & McGaghie, W. C.
design: Pretest-posttest study without a control group; residents were scored on 6 simulated ACLS scenarios against research-derived minimum passing scores (the mastery criterion), completed a minimum of four 2-hour simulation-based deliberate-practice sessions, and those not meeting the mastery standard received additional practice until criterion was reached, followed by a posttest 1-2 weeks after final training.
population: Second-year (PGY-2) internal medicine residents in a single residency program.
institution: Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine (Northwestern Memorial Hospital and Jesse Brown Veterans Affairs Medical Center)
outcome: Mean checklist performance rose from 72.2% (pretest) to 88.7% (posttest), a 24% absolute improvement (P<=.0001); 100% of residents (41/41) met or exceeded the mastery standard, with 80.5% doing so within the standard curriculum and 19.5% requiring 15 minutes to 1 hour of additional deliberate practice to reach criterion.
limitations: Single residency program at one academic medical center, relatively small sample (n=41), no untrained control group, and the same simulator was used for both training and testing, which could inflate apparent gains.
qualityRationale: Real-world criterion-referenced mastery learning trial with a clearly defined, research-derived mastery standard and objective performance data, but lacks a control group, is single-site, and used the same simulator for training and assessment, limiting causal and generalizability claims.

title: Using Tests to Enhance 8th Grade Students' Retention of U.S. History Facts
authors: Carpenter, S. K., Pashler, H., & Cepeda, N. J.
design: Classroom field experiment with a 2 (review timing: 1 week vs. 16 weeks after initial instruction) x 3 (review type: test with feedback, restudy, no review) mixed design; retention of previously taught U.S. history facts was assessed on a cumulative final test administered approximately 9 months (36 weeks) after initial instruction.
population: Eighth-grade students (44 female, 31 male; 62 analyzed after attrition: 29 in the 1-week/Immediate Review group, 33 in the 16-week/Delayed Review group) at a charter school in San Diego, California.
institution: University of California, San Diego (research team); charter school field site in San Diego, California
outcome: On the final test 9 months later, facts previously reviewed via testing were recalled significantly better than facts reviewed via restudying, and nearly twice as well as facts given no review (mean approximately 3.08 vs. 2.18 vs. 1.58, respectively); the 16-week (Delayed Review) group showed somewhat better overall retention than the 1-week (Immediate Review) group, though this difference only approached significance.
limitations: Authors note very low absolute retention after 9 months consistent with floor effects, that students were ungraded on and may not have expected the final test (potentially reducing motivation), and that the study examined only discrete factual questions rather than conceptual understanding, limiting generalizability.
qualityRationale: Genuine classroom field experiment with real students and a delayed 9-month retention outcome, strengthening ecological validity, but the analyzed sample is small (n=62) and single-school, retention scores were near floor, and the review-timing contrast was underpowered.

title: Impoverished cue support enhances subsequent retention: Support for the elaborative retrieval explanation of the testing effect
authors: Carpenter, S. K. & DeLosh, E. L.
design: Three-experiment lab study using within-/mixed-subjects designs manipulating the type and number of retrieval cues on intervening tests
population: Undergraduate students enrolled in introductory psychology at Colorado State University
outcome: Across three experiments, items retrieved with fewer retrieval cues (more elaborative retrieval) on an intervening test were better retained on the final test than items retrieved with more cues, supporting an elaborative-retrieval explanation of the testing effect.
limitations: Experiments used artificial eight-item word lists and short retention intervals (15 sec to 5 min between study and intervening test; 5 min final test) with college-student samples from a single institution.
qualityRationale: Well-controlled multi-experiment lab study with an internal replication, but relies on a single-institution undergraduate sample and short retention intervals.

title: Examining the testing effect with open- and closed-book tests
authors: Agarwal, P. K., Karpicke, J. D., Kang, S. H. K., Roediger, H. L. & McDermott, K. B.
design: Two within-subjects lab experiments comparing open-book, closed-book, restudy, and no-test control conditions, with a one-week delayed criterial test
population: Undergraduate students (ages 18-24) at Washington University in St. Louis
outcome: Both open-book and closed-book testing, when followed by feedback, produced a robust testing effect (better one-week retention than studying once or repeated restudying); the open-book immediate-test advantage vanished by the delayed test.
limitations: Materials were brief (~1000-word) expository prose passages studied in single one-hour lab sessions rather than authentic multi-week classroom courses.
qualityRationale: Controlled two-experiment lab study with a delayed one-week retention test and a within-subjects replication, but a single-institution convenience sample.

title: Is expanding retrieval a superior method for learning text materials?
authors: Karpicke, J. D. & Roediger, H. L.
design: Two lab experiments factorially crossing the position of the first retrieval test with the spacing schedule of repeated tests, with a one-week delayed final free-recall test
population: Washington University undergraduate students participating for course credit
institution: Purdue University; Washington University in St. Louis
outcome: Repeated retrieval practice produced large gains in one-week retention of text material over a single test or studying alone; there was no meaningful difference between expanding and equally spaced schedules of repeated retrieval on long-term retention.
limitations: Brief encyclopedia-style text passages and short spacing intervals (minutes) within single-session lab procedures with only Washington University undergraduates.
qualityRationale: Two-experiment lab study with a delayed retention test and a factorial design disentangling previously confounded variables, but single-institution undergraduate samples.

title: Learning Concepts and Categories: Is Spacing the "Enemy of Induction"?
authors: Kornell, N. & Bjork, R. A.
design: Multiple within- and between-subjects lab experiments manipulating massed vs. spaced (interleaved) presentation of exemplars during inductive category learning, with recognition/identification tests and metacognitive judgments
population: University of California, Los Angeles undergraduates
outcome: Spacing (interleaving) exemplars produced significantly better inductive learning than massing, even though participants overwhelmingly rated massed study as more effective -- a metacognitive illusion that persisted despite their own test performance showing the opposite.
limitations: One artificial domain (painting styles) with UCLA undergraduates in short single-session lab experiments; a control task showed spacing can hurt performance on single-answer tasks.
qualityRationale: Multiple converging lab experiments with built-in replications, but a single-institution sample and one narrow experimental domain.

title: Distributing Learning Over Time: The Spacing Effect in Children's Acquisition and Generalization of Science Concepts
authors: Vlach, H. A. & Sandhofer, C. M.
design: Randomized between-subjects experiment with three learning schedules (massed, clumped, spaced), using a pretest and a one-week delayed posttest
population: Early elementary school children aged 5 to 7 years recruited from a university laboratory school
outcome: Children who received four science lessons spaced one per day across four days showed significantly greater gains in both simple and complex generalization than children who received the lessons massed in a single day or clumped over two days.
limitations: Small sample (12 children per condition, N=36) from a single university laboratory school, and only one content domain (food chains).
qualityRationale: Randomized comparison of three learning schedules with a delayed posttest, but a small single-site sample limits statistical power.

title: Distributed and Massed Practice: From Laboratory to Classroom
authors: Seabrook, R., Brown, G. D. A. & Solity, J. E.
design: Two laboratory word-list recall experiments across five age groups and one between-subjects classroom quasi-experiment comparing distributed vs. clustered teaching of reading
population: UK schoolchildren aged 5-19 and university undergraduates (lab experiments); Year 1 primary schoolchildren from two schools (classroom study)
institution: Oxford Brookes University and University of Warwick, UK
outcome: Spacing (lag) benefits for word recall were equally strong across ages 5 through adult; in a real classroom study, children taught reading phonics in three short distributed daily sessions improved more than six times as much as children taught the same total time in one longer clustered daily session.
limitations: The classroom experiment was small (12 children per condition after matching) and compared only two teachers/schools, with only a 1-day retention interval before final testing.
qualityRationale: Combines converging lab experiments with a real classroom quasi-experiment using actual teachers and curricula, but small classroom sample limits causal certainty.

title: Cognitive Load Theory and the Format of Instruction
authors: Chandler, P. & Sweller, J.
design: Series of six between-subjects experiments comparing conventional split-source instructional materials against format-integrated materials
population: First-year trade apprentices with no prior formal electrical training (Sydney, Australia); later experiments used further apprentice cohorts and Year 9 high school science students
outcome: Materials that physically integrated related diagrams and text produced significantly better learning than conventional split-source formats when the material required mental integration of multiple interacting information sources; the advantage persisted across a 12-week retention interval.
limitations: No direct physiological or subjective cognitive-load measure was obtained in the realistic industrial-training setting; load/effort was inferred from performance outcomes rather than measured directly.
qualityRationale: Foundational primary cognitive-load-theory experiment across six converging studies including a real industrial-training setting with a 12-week retention check.

title: Reducing Cognitive Load by Mixing Auditory and Visual Presentation Modes
authors: Mousavi, S. Y., Low, R. & Sweller, J.
design: Series of six between-subjects experiments comparing purely visual/written presentation of geometry worked examples against a mixed auditory-and-visual presentation format
population: Australian elementary and secondary school students learning geometry
outcome: Mixed auditory-and-visual presentation of geometry worked examples reduced split-attention-related cognitive load and produced better problem-solving performance than a purely visual format, supporting partially independent auditory/visual working-memory resources.
limitations: The effect was tested only with geometry content and school-aged samples, so generalization to other domains, media formats, and adult learners was not directly established.
qualityRationale: Well-known primary multi-experiment study independently corroborated by an ERIC abstract reporting the same N and design.

title: The Effects of Interleaved Practice
authors: Taylor, K. & Rohrer, D.
design: Between-subjects experiment with random assignment to interleaved vs. blocked practice-problem ordering, followed by a delayed test
population: Fourth-grade students (ages 10-11) at an elementary school in St. Petersburg, Florida
outcome: Students who practiced four related types of math problems in interleaved order scored nearly double on a test given one day later (77% vs. 38%, d=1.21) compared to students who practiced in blocked order, even though interleaving impaired practice-session performance itself.
limitations: Retention interval tested was only one day, the four problem types were closely related, and possible ceiling/floor effects during blocked practice may have contributed to the size of the observed benefit.
qualityRationale: Highly-cited primary classroom experiment with random assignment and error-pattern analysis explaining the mechanism.

title: Learning Painting Styles: Spacing Is Advantageous When It Promotes Discriminative Contrast
authors: Kang, S. H. K. & Pashler, H.
design: Between-subjects laboratory experiments manipulating interleaved vs. massed (and temporally spaced vs. simultaneous) presentation of painting exemplars, followed by a transfer test classifying novel paintings by artist
population: Adult participants at the University of California, San Diego learning to identify painters' styles
outcome: Participants classified novel paintings by artist more accurately when training exemplars were interleaved across artists rather than massed, but increasing temporal spacing while keeping presentation blocked by artist did not improve performance, supporting a discriminative-contrast explanation of the interleaving benefit rather than general temporal spacing.
limitations: A specific inductive category-learning task with a limited number of artists and exemplars per condition, limiting generalization to other induction domains and longer retention intervals.
qualityRationale: DOI identity and metadata confirmed via Crossref and Semantic Scholar; graded B as full-text access relied on a secondary mirror rather than the publisher page.

title: Delayed versus immediate feedback in children's and adults' vocabulary learning
authors: Metcalfe, J., Kornell, N. & Finn, B.
design: Two multi-session experiments manipulating timing of corrective feedback (delayed vs. immediate vs. no feedback) during vocabulary study, with retention interval to final test both controlled and uncontrolled across conditions
population: Grade 6 children (Experiment 1, n=18) and college undergraduates (Experiment 2, n=20)
outcome: Grade 6 children retained more school-relevant vocabulary with delayed than immediate feedback even when retention interval was controlled; college students showed a delayed-feedback advantage only when retention interval was uncontrolled, disappearing once lag to test was equated.
limitations: Experiment 1's final children's sample was small (18 of 27 recruited, due to exclusions), and the diverging pattern between children and adults suggests the benefit may not generalize across age groups.
qualityRationale: Real experimental manipulation of feedback timing with a controlled-lag design, but a small usable child sample and diverging age-group results.

title: Delaying feedback promotes transfer of knowledge despite student preferences to receive feedback immediately
authors: Mullet, H. G., Butler, A. C., Verdin, B., von Borries, R. & Marsh, E. J.
design: Two field experiments in an authentic undergraduate engineering course manipulating feedback timing (immediate vs. 1-week delayed) on weekly homework
population: Undergraduate students in an upper-level engineering signals-and-systems course
venue: Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition
institution: University of Texas at El Paso; Duke University
outcome: Students who received delayed feedback on weekly homework scored higher on subsequent transfer exam problems than those given immediate feedback (Experiment 1: d=0.75), replicated in Experiment 2, even though most students reported preferring immediate feedback.
limitations: Immediate feedback was released after the assignment deadline rather than instantaneously; the classroom setting could not control for confounds such as lectures or group study, and analyses were somewhat underpowered given modest class sizes.
qualityRationale: Ecologically valid field experiment in a real course measuring transfer to novel exam problems, replicated across two experiments with an honest discussion of confounds.

title: Generating keywords improves metacomprehension and self-regulation in elementary and middle school children
authors: de Bruin, A. B. H., Thiede, K. W., Camp, G. & Redford, J. S.
design: Two experiments testing whether generating keywords at a delay (vs. no keyword generation) before making comprehension judgments improved children's metacomprehension accuracy and subsequent restudy self-regulation
population: Fourth grade (n=85) and sixth grade (n=66) children (Experiment 1), and seventh grade children (n=94, Experiment 2)
institution: Boise State University; Maastricht University; Erasmus University Rotterdam
outcome: For sixth and seventh graders, generating delayed keywords before judging comprehension significantly improved metacomprehension accuracy relative to a no-keyword control; improved metacomprehension accuracy was associated with improved regulation of subsequent study. Fourth graders showed no benefit.
limitations: The keyword-generation benefit did not emerge for the youngest children (fourth graders), suggesting the strategy's effectiveness is developmentally constrained.
qualityRationale: Large, well-powered sample (N=245) across two experiments and three grade levels, with a concrete behavioral intervention and a documented developmental boundary condition.

title: Training self-assessment and task-selection skills: A cognitive approach to improving self-regulated learning
authors: Kostons, D., van Gog, T. & Paas, F.
design: Two experiments in biology problem-solving testing whether observing a modeled example of self-assessment/task-selection, or practice, improved secondary students' acquisition of self-regulated learning skills
population: Secondary education students (Experiment 1 n=80, Experiment 2 n=90)
institution: University of Groningen / Open University of the Netherlands; Erasmus University Rotterdam; University of Wollongong
outcome: Training self-assessment and task-selection skills, whether via modeled examples or practice, significantly improved students' accuracy in these skills and increased knowledge gained during subsequent self-regulated learning where students chose their own tasks.
limitations: Training and its benefits were tested only within a single content domain (biology problem-solving); transfer to other academic domains was not established.
qualityRationale: Two well-powered experiments with an explicit skills-training manipulation and measured downstream self-regulated-learning gains, though single-domain.

title: Intrinsic Motivation and the Process of Learning: Beneficial Effects of Contextualization, Personalization, and Choice
authors: Cordova, D. I. & Lepper, M. R.
design: Randomized experiment (control plus four conditions: contextualization, personalization, choice, combined) using a computer-based arithmetic order-of-operations task
population: Fourth- and fifth-grade elementary school students
outcome: Contextualization, personalization, and provision of choice each increased students' intrinsic motivation, depth of engagement, amount learned in a fixed time period, and perceived competence relative to control.
limitations: Small sample (N=72) from a single elementary age band and a single computer-based arithmetic task, limiting generalizability to other subjects and formats.
qualityRationale: True experimental design with random assignment to conditions in a top-tier peer-reviewed journal; a classic, widely-replicated primary study on autonomy/choice and intrinsic motivation.

title: Engaging Students in Learning Activities: It Is Not Autonomy Support or Structure But Autonomy Support and Structure
authors: Jang, H., Reeve, J. & Deci, E. L.
design: Field study using trained-observer ratings of teachers' instructional style (autonomy support, structure) and students' behavioral engagement, combined with student self-reported engagement, analyzed with hierarchical linear modeling across classrooms
population: High school students in Grades 9-11 across 133 public high school classrooms
institution: University of Rochester; Korea University; Hanyang University
outcome: Student engagement was highest when teachers provided high levels of both autonomy support and structure together; the two instructional qualities functioned as complementary rather than antagonistic predictors of engagement.
limitations: Correlational field design without experimental manipulation of teacher style limits causal inference; sample drawn from a single U.S. Midwest region and only Grades 9-11.
qualityRationale: Large-sample (N=1,584, 133 classrooms) field study combining independent observer ratings and student self-report in a top-tier peer-reviewed journal.

title: Test Anxiety and Academic Performance in Undergraduate and Graduate Students
authors: Chapell, M. S., Blanding, Z. B., Silverstein, M. E., Takahashi, M., Newman, B., Gubi, A. & McCann, N.
design: Correlational survey study relating self-reported trait test anxiety to GPA, stratified by gender and educational level
population: University students: 4,000 undergraduates and 1,414 graduate students
topic: anxiety, frustration and confidence in learning
outcome: A significant but small inverse relationship was found between test anxiety and GPA in both undergraduate and graduate students; low-test-anxious undergraduates averaged a B+ versus a B for high-test-anxious students, with additional gender-differentiated effects among graduate students.
limitations: Correlational design precludes causal conclusions; the anxiety-performance relationship, while statistically significant given the very large sample, was described as small in magnitude.
qualityRationale: Very large sample (N=5,414) primary survey study in a top-tier journal; graded B because the design is correlational and single-institution.

title: Test Anxiety and GCSE Performance: The Effect of Gender and Socio-Economic Background
authors: Putwain, D. W.
design: Correlational study using hierarchical regression relating trait test anxiety to GCSE examination performance, with gender and socio-economic background as moderators
population: Mixed-ability Year 11 secondary school students in the UK from three secondary schools
topic: anxiety, frustration and confidence in learning
outcome: A small but significant inverse relationship was found between trait test anxiety and GCSE examination performance, with the cognitive (worry) component accounting for about 7% of performance variance; the relationship was moderated by socio-economic background but not gender.
limitations: Cross-sectional correlational design limits causal inference; sample confined to three secondary schools in one UK region, and anxiety explained only a small proportion of variance.
qualityRationale: Primary field study with a reasonably large sample across three schools; graded B because the design is correlational and the effect size is small.

title: All Other Things Being Equal: Acquisition and Transfer of the Control of Variables Strategy
authors: Chen, Z. & Klahr, D.
design: Controlled training experiment in which children received explicit domain-specific training in the Control of Variables Strategy (CVS) combined with probe questions, or probe questions alone; near- and far-transfer to novel, untrained problem domains was assessed
population: Children aged 7 to 10 years
institution: University of California, Davis; Carnegie Mellon University
outcome: Children who received explicit training in CVS combined with probe questions learned and transferred the strategy to novel, untrained domains; probe questions alone without explicit direct instruction did not reliably produce acquisition or transfer.
limitations: Single cross-sectional age range tested with a laboratory probe-based training paradigm rather than typical extended classroom instruction, with a limited set of novel-domain transfer problems.
qualityRationale: Well-known controlled experiment in a top developmental-psychology journal directly manipulating training conditions and measuring transfer to novel domains.

title: Promoting Transfer: Effects of Self-Explanation and Direct Instruction
authors: Rittle-Johnson, B.
design: Randomized 2x2 between-subjects experiment (direct instruction vs. invention of a procedure, crossed with self-explanation vs. no explanation) with children learning mathematical equivalence; transfer to novel problem types was assessed after the instructional session
population: Third- through fifth-grade children, ages 8-11
outcome: Self-explanation promoted transfer of the learned procedure to novel problem types regardless of whether children received direct instruction or invented the procedure themselves; both self-explanation and instruction independently improved learning and retention of the correct procedure.
limitations: Single content domain (mathematical equivalence) and a short single-session training procedure, so generalization to other subjects or extended classroom instruction is untested.
qualityRationale: Randomized factorial experiment in a top developmental-psychology journal with a clearly defined transfer outcome measure.

title: Repeated Retrieval During Learning Is the Key to Long-Term Retention
authors: Karpicke, J. D. & III, H. L. R.
design: Two laboratory experiments manipulating repeated study vs. repeated retrieval practice during learning, and continued vs. dropped practice of items already recalled once (a recall-based mastery/removal criterion); final cued-recall retention test administered one week after the learning session
population: Undergraduate students
outcome: Repeated retrieval practice during learning produced far greater one-week retention than repeated restudying. Dropping items already recalled once from further restudy gave no retention cost, whereas dropping them from further retrieval practice cut final recall by more than half relative to continued retrieval.
limitations: Undergraduate sample learning laboratory word-pair materials under controlled single-session conditions, limiting generalization to authentic classroom content and longer retention intervals.
qualityRationale: Highly-cited two-experiment lab study directly manipulating a recall-criterion (mastery-based) practice-removal rule with a delayed retention test.

title: Testing Versus Review: Effects on Retention
authors: Nungester, R. J. & Duchastel, P. C.
design: Three-group experiment: after reading a brief history passage, high-school seniors either took an initial test on the passage, spent equivalent time reviewing it, or performed an unrelated filler task; a delayed retention test was administered two weeks later
population: High school seniors
outcome: On the test given two weeks later, students who had taken an initial test on the passage retained more than those who reviewed the passage or performed an unrelated task; the testing benefit was specific to the tested content regardless of initial test format.
limitations: Single sample of high-school seniors, a single content domain (one history passage), and a single two-week retention interval, limiting generalization.
qualityRationale: Classic, widely-cited foundational testing-effect study with a clear delayed-assessment design, but an older paper with a single population and content domain.

title: Adaptive Memory: Survival Processing Enhances Retention
authors: Nairne, J. S., Thompson, S. R. & Pandeirada, J. N. S.
design: Four incidental-learning experiments (Experiment 1 between-subjects; Experiments 2-4 within-subject) in which participants rated words for survival relevance vs. control scenarios, followed by a surprise free-recall or recognition retention test
population: Purdue University undergraduates enrolled in introductory psychology
venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
outcome: Words processed for survival relevance were retained significantly better than the same words processed for pleasantness, relocation relevance, or self-reference; the advantage held across free recall and recognition and across between- and within-subject designs.
limitations: The authors compared survival processing with only a limited set of control conditions and did not directly compare with unrelated words matched on other dimensions, so the precise mechanism and full generality remain unestablished.
qualityRationale: Four converging experiments (between- and within-subject) with random assignment, established control conditions, and a large combined sample.

title: Replication and Analysis of Ebbinghaus' Forgetting Curve
authors: Murre, J. M. J. & Dros, J.
design: Single-subject replication of Ebbinghaus' method-of-savings forgetting-curve experiment: the subject learned lists of nonsense syllables and relearned them after retention intervals from 20 minutes to 31 days, compared against Ebbinghaus' original data and two other historical replications
population: One 22-year-old Dutch male adult undergoing 70 hours of learning/relearning sessions
outcome: The replication reproduced Ebbinghaus' classic power-function forgetting curve using the savings method, but also found an upward jump in savings starting at the 24-hour retention interval, suggesting a sleep-related memory benefit not present in the original 1880s data.
limitations: Single-subject (N=1) design severely limits generalizability; only 10 word lists per retention interval were used versus 12-45 in Ebbinghaus' original, and time-of-day of testing could not be fully controlled.
qualityRationale: Rigorous, peer-reviewed direct replication of a foundational forgetting-curve paradigm with transparent methodology, but a single-subject design sharply limits generalizability.

title: Factors Predicting the Use of Technology: Findings From the Center for Research and Education on Aging and Technology Enhancement (CREATE)
authors: Czaja, S. J., Charness, N., Fisk, A. D., Hertzog, C., Nair, S. N., Rogers, W. A. & Sharit, J.
design: Cross-sectional correlational study using hierarchical multiple regression and structural equation modeling to test whether computer anxiety, computer self-efficacy, and cognitive abilities mediate age differences in technology adoption and use
population: Community-dwelling adults aged 18-91, ethnically diverse, recruited from Miami, Atlanta, and Tallahassee areas
institution: University of Miami (CREATE consortium, with Georgia Institute of Technology and Florida State University)
outcome: Older adults reported significantly lower technology, computer, and Internet use than younger age groups; computer anxiety and fluid/crystallized cognitive abilities partially mediated these age differences, but substantial direct effects of age on technology use remained.
limitations: The sample was relatively healthy and well-educated for its age range, which likely underestimates the true magnitude of age-related barriers to technology use in the broader older-adult population.
qualityRationale: Large (N=1204), multi-site, ethnically and age-diverse sample with an explicit mediation model of cognitive and attitudinal predictors of age-related technology use.

title: Training Older Adults to Use Automatic Teller Machines
authors: Rogers, W. A., Fisk, A. D., Mead, S. E., Walker, N. & Cabrera, E. F.
design: Randomized between-subjects experiment with four training-format conditions (general overview only, written text guide, pictorial guide, interactive online tutorial); after a 24-hour retention interval, participants performed familiar and novel ATM transactions on an unfamiliar simulator
population: Older adults aged 61-81, randomly assigned to four groups of 14 participants each
venue: Human Factors: The Journal of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society
institution: Georgia Institute of Technology; University of Georgia
outcome: The interactive online tutorial, which provided specific practice on task components, produced the best skill acquisition and transfer to novel transactions, followed by the pictorial guide and text guide, with the description-only overview producing the weakest performance.
limitations: The study included only older adults (61-81) with no younger-adult comparison group, so the findings cannot establish whether the training-format advantage is specific to older learners.
qualityRationale: Well-controlled randomized experiment with a clear, real-world accessibility task, but a modest sample and no younger-adult comparison group.

title: Setting, elaborating, and reflecting on personal goals improves academic performance
authors: Morisano, D., Hirsh, J. B., Peterson, J. B., Pihl, R. O. & Shore, B. M.
design: Randomized controlled trial: intensive online written goal-setting, elaboration, and reflection program vs. an active control task
population: Academically struggling undergraduate students at a Canadian university
outcome: Students randomly assigned to the goal-setting intervention showed significantly greater improvement in academic performance (GPA) over the following 4 months than students who completed an active control task of equivalent face validity.
limitations: Single-institution volunteer sample of academically struggling undergraduates; outcomes tracked only over a 4-month follow-up window, so longer-term durability is untested.
qualityRationale: Peer-reviewed RCT with random assignment, an active control condition, and a real academic-performance outcome, directly relevant to goal-setting/progress-review design.

title: Less stick more carrot? Increasing the uptake of deposit contract financial incentives for physical activity: A randomized controlled trial
authors: Buisonjé, D. R. D., Reijnders, T., Rodrigues, T. R. C., Santhanam, P., Kowatsch, T., Breeman, L. D., Janssen, V. R., Kraaijenhagen, R. A., Kemps, H. M. & Evers, A. W.
design: Randomized controlled trial using a smartphone app with daily step-goal tracking and progress feedback, crossed with deposit-contract incentive framing/customization
population: Healthy university students (mean age 21.6 years), the Netherlands
outcome: Daily physical-activity goal-progress feedback combined with deposit-contract incentives produced high uptake (83.2%) and goal achievement (about 14.9 of 20 daily goals met); matched deposits raised uptake odds substantially, while a customizable deposit amount did not improve, and could reduce, effectiveness.
limitations: Sample restricted to healthy Dutch university students, limiting generalizability; the customizable-deposit condition may have reduced effectiveness when deposits went unmatched.
qualityRationale: Preregistered RCT in a peer-reviewed sport/exercise psychology journal with a real tracked behavioral outcome (daily activity-goal attainment) in a healthy, non-clinical population.

title: Exercise habit formation in new gym members: a longitudinal study
authors: Kaushal, N. & Rhodes, R. E.
design: Longitudinal field survey study (12 weeks) with self-report habit-strength and behavior measures, analyzed via linear mixed-model trajectory analysis
population: New gym members, Canada
outcome: Exercising at least 4 times per week for about 6 weeks was the approximate minimum needed to establish an exercise habit; habit and intention functioned as parallel predictors of continued exercise, and consistency, low behavioral complexity, favorable environment, and positive affective judgments predicted habit strength.
limitations: Relies on self-reported exercise behavior and habit-strength surveys from a single cohort of gym members, limiting generalizability beyond gym-based exercise contexts.
qualityRationale: Peer-reviewed prospective longitudinal field study of real behavior-tracking in a healthy, non-clinical population with a concrete, actionable threshold for healthy habit formation.

title: Forming a flossing habit: An exploratory study of the psychological determinants of habit formation
authors: Judah, G., Gardner, B. & Aunger, R.
design: Prospective field intervention study with daily self-report diaries, automaticity measured at 4 weeks, follow-up at 8 months; between-subjects manipulation of habit-cue timing (flossing before vs. after toothbrushing)
population: Adult volunteers, London, UK
institution: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, UK
outcome: Stronger prospective memory, higher levels of past behavior, and more positive attitudes predicted increased flossing frequency; participants cued to floss after brushing developed stronger, more automatic habits than those cued to floss before brushing, with differences persisting at 8-month follow-up.
limitations: Small (N=50), single-group exploratory design without a no-intervention control group.
qualityRationale: Peer-reviewed prospective field study directly measuring healthy cue-routine habit formation and its automaticity growth curve; graded B for its small sample and lack of a no-intervention comparison arm.

title: Putting category learning in order: Category structure and temporal arrangement affect the benefit of interleaved over blocked study
authors: Carvalho, P. F. & Goldstone, R. L.
design: Multi-experiment lab study manipulating study order (interleaved vs. blocked) and category structure (high vs. low within-category similarity) during category learning, with a later classification test
population: Undergraduate students
outcome: The benefit of interleaved over blocked study depended on category structure: interleaving helped most when categories were easily confusable (low between-category, high within-category similarity), while blocking could help when categories were highly distinct.
limitations: Used artificial perceptual categories (bird/butterfly images) in single lab sessions, limiting generalization to real classroom subject matter and longer retention intervals.
qualityRationale: Peer-reviewed multi-experiment lab study directly manipulating interleaving and category structure, but single-site with artificial stimuli.

title: Why does interleaving improve math learning? The contributions of discriminative contrast and distributed practice
authors: Foster, N. L., Mueller, M. L., Was, C., Rawson, K. A. & Dunlosky, J.
design: Classroom-based experiment disentangling the discriminative-contrast and distributed-practice components of interleaved mathematics practice using a 2x2 design (interleaved/blocked x same-day/spaced)
population: Middle-school students
outcome: Both discriminative contrast and distributed practice contributed independently to the interleaving benefit for math problem-solving, with the fully interleaved-and-spaced condition producing the best performance.
limitations: Single school district sample and one mathematics topic domain, limiting generalization across subjects and populations.
qualityRationale: Controlled classroom experiment cleanly separating two theoretical mechanisms of interleaving with objective math-test outcomes.

title: The exemplar interleaving effect in inductive learning: Moderation by the difficulty of category discriminations
authors: Zulkiply, N. & Burt, J. S.
design: Multi-experiment lab study comparing interleaved vs. blocked presentation of category exemplars across categories varying in discrimination difficulty, with a later classification test
population: University students
institution: Universiti Sains Malaysia; University of New South Wales
outcome: Interleaving improved inductive category learning relative to blocking, and the benefit was moderated by discrimination difficulty, replicating and extending prior induction-interleaving findings to new category sets.
limitations: Artificial visual-art category stimuli in single lab sessions limit generalization to real academic category learning.
qualityRationale: Multi-experiment controlled lab replication directly testing interleaving benefits and their moderators.

title: Guidance during mathematical problem solving
authors: Tarmizi, R. A. & Sweller, J.
design: Series of lab experiments comparing conventional means-ends problem solving to worked-example study for geometry problems, testing for a split-attention effect when diagrams and text were physically separated
population: Secondary-school students
outcome: When diagrams and explanatory text were physically separated (requiring split attention), the usual worked-example advantage over conventional problem solving disappeared or reversed, consistent with a cognitive-load account of the split-attention effect.
limitations: Small single-site secondary-school sample restricted to geometry problems, limiting generalization to other content domains.
qualityRationale: Controlled multi-experiment lab study directly testing a cognitive-load mechanism (split attention) with objective performance outcomes.

title: The Use of Worked Examples as a Substitute for Problem Solving in Learning Algebra
authors: Sweller, J. & Cooper, G. A.
design: Two lab experiments comparing conventional problem-solving practice to alternating worked-example/problem-pair study for learning algebraic transformations
population: Ninth-grade secondary-school students
outcome: Students who studied worked examples paired with problems solved subsequent problems faster and with fewer errors than students who solved an equivalent number of problems without worked examples, establishing the foundational worked-example effect attributed to reduced cognitive load.
limitations: Small, single-site sample restricted to one algebra topic (algebraic transformations) and short-term outcomes only.
qualityRationale: Foundational controlled classroom-relevant experiment establishing the worked-example effect via a cognitive-load mechanism.

title: A comparison of three measures of cognitive load: Evidence for separable measures of intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load
authors: DeLeeuw, K. E. & Mayer, R. E.
design: Lab experiment using three converging measures (response time to a secondary task, mental-effort rating, difficulty rating) across multimedia-learning materials manipulating intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load separately
population: Undergraduate students
outcome: The three cognitive-load measures were differentially sensitive to the three theorized load types (intrinsic, extraneous, germane), supporting cognitive load theory's tripartite structure rather than a single undifferentiated load construct.
limitations: Single-session lab study with university students and short multimedia lessons, limiting generalization to sustained classroom instruction.
qualityRationale: Controlled lab experiment with converging behavioral and self-report measures directly testing the structure of cognitive load theory.

title: Timing Matters: The Impact of Immediate and Delayed Feedback on Artificial Language Learning
authors: Opitz, B., Ferdinand, N. K. & Mecklinger, A.
design: Two-experiment, between-subjects lab study using event-related potentials (ERP) with an artificial grammar learning task; participants classified non-word strings and received visual feedback either immediately or after a 1-second delay
population: German-speaking university students, native German speakers with normal/corrected vision and no neurological/psychiatric history
outcome: Both immediate- and delayed-feedback groups learned the artificial grammar, but the performance gain was significantly larger for the immediate-feedback group than the delayed-feedback group.
limitations: Small sample (45 analyzed) of young German university students in an artificial, non-linguistic laboratory task, limiting generalizability to real classroom feedback.
qualityRationale: Controlled, randomized-condition lab experiment with objective ERP/behavioral measures, but small single-site sample and an artificial (non-classroom) learning task.

title: The benefits of computer-generated feedback for mathematics problem solving
authors: Fyfe, E. R. & Rittle-Johnson, B.
design: Randomized experiment embedded in a classroom setting; children received strategy instruction then were randomly assigned to no feedback, immediate feedback, or summative feedback from a computer while solving math-equivalence problems, with a posttest the next day
population: Second-grade children from one public and one private elementary school, screened to have low initial mastery of math equivalence
outcome: Feedback (vs. no feedback) raised posttest scores for children with low prior knowledge; immediate feedback was most effective, producing mastery for children with both low and high prior knowledge.
limitations: Two-school convenience sample restricted to second graders and a single math-equivalence topic; only one delayed retention point (next-day posttest) was measured.
qualityRationale: Randomized, controlled experiment with random assignment to feedback conditions and an independent posttest, run in an authentic classroom population.

title: Learning from feedback: Spacing and the delay-retention effect
authors: Smith, T. A. & Kimball, D. R.
design: Two within/between-subjects lab experiments manipulating feedback timing (immediate vs. delayed) and study/test/feedback lags during cued recall of trivia facts, testing competing theoretical accounts of the delay-retention effect
population: Undergraduate students (121 in Experiment 1, 81 in Experiment 2)
venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
outcome: Delaying feedback increased the probability that initially correct responses persevered on a later retention test but had minimal effect on error correction, supporting a spacing-of-encoding-opportunities account rather than a pure error-correction account of feedback timing.
limitations: Used artificial trivia-fact cued-recall materials rather than authentic classroom content, and undergraduate-only samples limit generalization to other learner populations.
qualityRationale: Two well-controlled lab experiments manipulating feedback timing directly, though limited to undergraduate samples and artificial verbal-learning materials.

title: Direct instruction of metacognition benefits adolescent science learning, transfer, and motivation: An in vivo study
authors: Zepeda, C. D., Richey, J. E., Ronevich, P. & Nokes-Malach, T. J.
design: Randomized controlled in-vivo classroom experiment; students randomly assigned to a control group (extensive problem-solving practice only) or an experimental group receiving a 6-hour intervention teaching declarative/procedural planning, monitoring and evaluation skills alongside more limited practice
population: Eighth-grade middle-school science students
outcome: The metacognitive-instruction group showed greater gains in metacognition, learning, transfer to novel problems, and motivation than the control group, despite receiving less problem-solving practice time.
limitations: Small single-school sample of eighth graders in one science domain, limiting generalizability across ages, subjects, and school contexts.
qualityRationale: Randomized controlled trial with random assignment to intervention vs. control condition and objective learning/transfer measures in an authentic classroom (in vivo) setting.

title: Evidence that judgments of learning are causally related to study choice
authors: Metcalfe, J. & Finn, B.
design: Within/between-subjects lab experiments dissociating judgments of learning (JOLs) from actual recall/past-test performance (using illusory-JOL manipulations) to test whether study choices track JOLs or track prior performance
population: Columbia University and Barnard College undergraduate students
outcome: Participants' restudy choices tracked their (sometimes illusory) judgments of learning rather than their actual recall or past test performance, providing direct causal evidence that JOLs drive study-choice behavior.
limitations: Small, single-institution undergraduate samples in artificial paired-associate word-list tasks; findings may not generalize to real academic study materials or other learner populations.
qualityRationale: Well-controlled multi-experiment lab study directly manipulating the JOL-recall dissociation, though small undergraduate samples and artificial memory materials limit external validity.

title: The effect of distributed monitoring exercises and feedback on performance, monitoring accuracy, and self-efficacy
authors: Nietfeld, J. L., Cao, L. & Osborne, J. W.
design: Quasi-experimental classroom study comparing an intact treatment class (given post-class self-assessment exercises and confidence-judgment review questions with feedback after every class) to an intact comparison class over a 16-week undergraduate course, with path analysis of performance, calibration, and self-efficacy
population: Undergraduate students in an educational psychology course (45 treatment, 39 comparison)
institution: North Carolina State University; University of West Georgia
outcome: The distributed monitoring-exercise-plus-feedback intervention significantly improved course performance, monitoring/calibration accuracy, and self-efficacy relative to the comparison class across the semester.
limitations: Quasi-experimental design used intact, non-randomly-assigned classes at a single institution, so treatment/comparison groups could differ on unmeasured pre-existing factors.
qualityRationale: Semester-long controlled classroom study with a comparison group and repeated objective outcome measures, but non-random assignment of intact class sections makes it a quasi-experiment rather than an RCT.

title: Autonomy in children's learning: An experimental and individual difference investigation
authors: Grolnick, W. S. & Ryan, R. M.
design: Randomized laboratory experiment (directed-learning vs. noncontrolling/autonomy-supportive directed-learning vs. nondirected spontaneous-learning conditions) combined with an individual-difference measure of children's autonomy orientation and an 8-day delayed-recall follow-up
population: Fifth-grade elementary school children (U.S.)
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
outcome: Both directed conditions produced more rote learning than the nondirected condition, but the noncontrolling (autonomy-supportive) directed condition produced better conceptual learning, greater interest, and less pressured affect than the controlling directed condition; children high in autonomy orientation retained more 8 days later.
limitations: Single age cohort (fifth graders) and a brief laboratory learning task, limiting generalization to sustained real classroom instruction.
qualityRationale: Peer-reviewed randomized controlled laboratory experiment with a delayed-retention follow-up, published in a top-tier psychology journal.

title: Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance
authors: Mueller, C. M. & Dweck, C. S.
design: Six randomized experiments manipulating type of praise (intelligence vs. effort vs. control) after success on a problem-solving task, then measuring goal choice, attributions, persistence, enjoyment, and performance after an induced failure
population: Fifth-grade children, ages 9-12, from Midwestern and Northeastern U.S. public schools
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
outcome: Children praised for intelligence adopted more performance goals, showed less persistence and enjoyment, performed worse after failure, and were more likely to misrepresent their scores than children praised for effort, who showed a more incremental view of intelligence and greater resilience.
limitations: All six studies used a single novel laboratory task administered individually, so findings may not generalize to repeated real classroom assignments.
qualityRationale: Six internally-replicated randomized controlled experiments (combined N=412) with consistent effects across independent child samples, published in a top-tier peer-reviewed journal.

title: Reappraising Stress Arousal Improves Performance and Reduces Evaluation Anxiety in Classroom Exam Situations
authors: Jamieson, J. P., Peters, B. J., Greenwood, E. J. & Altose, A. J.
design: Randomized double-blind field experiment in real community-college classrooms; students randomly assigned within classroom to stress-reappraisal vs. placebo-control instructions before their second in-class exam, with math anxiety, stress appraisals, and exam performance measured before and after
population: Developmental (remedial) mathematics students at an urban Midwestern community college
institution: University of Rochester; Cuyahoga Community College
topic: anxiety, frustration and confidence in learning
outcome: Students who reappraised stress arousal as adaptive reported less math evaluation anxiety and increased coping-resource appraisals, and scored significantly higher on their subsequent exam than placebo-control students; effects on grades persisted marginally to end-of-semester.
limitations: No direct physiological measure of stress was collected (self-report appraisals only), and the sample came from a single instructor/curriculum at one community college, limiting generalizability.
qualityRationale: Randomized double-blind field experiment conducted in real classrooms with objective exam-performance outcomes, published in a peer-reviewed journal.

title: The role of expressive writing in math anxiety
authors: Park, D., Ramirez, G. & Beilock, S. L.
design: Randomized laboratory experiment; students varying in trait math anxiety were assigned to write expressively about their thoughts/feelings regarding an upcoming math test or to sit quietly (control) before completing difficulty-matched math problems
population: University undergraduate students varying in math anxiety
topic: anxiety, frustration and confidence in learning
outcome: The expressive-writing intervention narrowed the math-performance gap between high- and low-math-anxious students; among highly math-anxious students, those whose writing contained more anxiety-related words showed the largest performance gains.
limitations: Single brief lab-based math task rather than a classroom exam, and the sample was restricted to university undergraduates, limiting generalization to other ages/settings.
qualityRationale: Peer-reviewed randomized controlled laboratory experiment with an a priori moderator (trait math anxiety) analysis.

title: Get excited: Reappraising pre-performance anxiety as excitement
authors: Brooks, A. W.
design: Series of randomized experiments manipulating anxiety-reappraisal self-statements/instructions before karaoke singing, public speaking, and math-test performance, with self-report, behavioral, and observer-rated outcomes and a mediation test of threat-vs-opportunity mind-set
population: Undergraduate students at a northeastern U.S. university
topic: anxiety, frustration and confidence in learning
outcome: Reappraising pre-performance anxiety as excitement (e.g., stating "I am excited") increased subjective excitement, self-efficacy/confidence, and objective performance relative to reappraising anxiety as calmness or not reappraising at all; the effect was mediated by an opportunity (vs. threat) mind-set.
limitations: All studies used single brief performance tasks in a lab setting with young-adult university students, so durability of the effect and generalization to real high-stakes academic assessments over time remain untested.
qualityRationale: Multiple internally-replicated randomized controlled experiments across three distinct performance domains with a tested mediating mechanism, published in a top-tier peer-reviewed journal.

title: Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: an experimental training study
authors: Schuster, C., Stebner, F., Leutner, D. & Wirth, J.
design: Randomized controlled training study; students randomly assigned to six conditions (two hybrid metacognitive+cognitive-strategy trainings, two non-hybrid cognitive-strategy-only trainings, two controls) across a 15-week intervention, with near- and far-transfer of metacognitive skills assessed post-training
population: Fifth-grade school students, Germany
institution: Ruhr University Bochum; University of Duisburg-Essen, Germany
outcome: Hybrid training (metacognitive skills + cognitive strategy), compared with non-hybrid and control training, improved students' near transfer (to similar learning tasks) and far transfer (to a new, untrained cognitive strategy) of metacognitive skills, though overall metacognitive-skill use remained low.
limitations: Metacognitive skills were scored quantitatively (amount of strategy talk) rather than qualitatively, and content-knowledge acquisition was not measured alongside transfer.
qualityRationale: Randomized assignment to six training conditions with a substantial school-based sample and a pre-registered near/far transfer design supports a Grade A classroom RCT.

title: Promoting learning transfer in science through a complexity approach and computational modeling
authors: Saba, J., Hel-Or, H. & Levy, S. T.
design: Quasi-experimental pretest-intervention-posttest comparison-group design; experimental group built computational models emphasizing complexity/systems features, compared to a comparison group, with near- and far-transfer science assessments
population: Seventh-grade middle school students, Israel
outcome: The experimental (computational-modeling) group showed significantly higher near-transfer performance and a medium-effect-size advantage in far transfer relative to the comparison group; computational thinking and systems understanding each independently predicted far transfer.
limitations: COVID-19 reduced the intervention from 6 to 4 sessions, likely limiting the far-transfer effect size; small sample; quasi-experimental design with different instructors per group introduces possible instructor confound.
qualityRationale: Peer-reviewed quasi-experimental comparison-group classroom study, but non-randomized, small (N=50), and instructor-confounded, placing it at Grade B.

title: An investigation of far and near transfer in a gamified visual learning paradigm
authors: Duyck, S. & Op de Beeck, H.
design: Randomized controlled trial with active control; experimental group completed 10 hours of gamified perceptual learning, active control group played 10 hours of Candy Crush Saga, with near- and far-transfer cognitive/attentional tasks tested pre- and post-training
population: Healthy non-gamer adults with normal or corrected-to-normal vision, Belgium
outcome: Far transfer occurred in some domains (executive functioning, mental rotation, multitasking) but equally in both trained and active-control groups; near transfer to novel-object categorization was more pronounced in the trained group, but most near-transfer measures did not exceed control-group improvement.
limitations: Small, underpowered sample (N=32) limits detection of true transfer effects; 10-hour training duration may be insufficient to produce robust transfer.
qualityRationale: Randomized design with an active control is a strength, but the very small, underpowered sample (N=32) keeps this at Grade B rather than A.

title: The Learning Benefits of Mastery Quizzing Versus Other Quizzing Methods
authors: Bates, L. E., Myers, S. J., DeLosh, E. L. & Rhodes, M. G.
design: Four randomized experiments comparing 'mastery quizzing' (repeated quizzing with feedback until a perfect score is reached) against standard single-pass and other quizzing conditions, with retention assessed on a later final test
population: Online adult volunteers, ages 18-76, not screened for prior content knowledge, United States
institution: Colorado State University; Chatham University; Minnesota State University, Mankato
outcome: Across all four experiments, final-test performance was better after mastery quizzing (continuing until a perfect quiz score with feedback) than after comparison quizzing methods that did not require a mastery criterion.
limitations: Participants were unscreened online volunteers rather than students in an actual course, and the materials were short psychology-concept passages rather than full classroom curricula.
qualityRationale: Four randomized experiments with a large combined sample (N=952) replicating the same effect qualify this as a Grade A controlled experimental study.

title: Separate mnemonic effects of retrieval practice and elaborative encoding
authors: Karpicke, J. D. & Smith, M. A.
design: Four between-subjects lab experiments; subjects learned word pairs to a one-correct-recall mastery criterion, then received repeated-study, repeated-elaboration, or repeated-retrieval trials, with long-term retention assessed on a delayed criterial test administered 1 week after initial learning
population: Undergraduate students
outcome: After items were learned to a one-correct-recall criterion, repeated retrieval produced better long-term retention on the 1-week delayed test than repeated restudying or repeated elaborative encoding, even when elaboration was directly and successfully induced during additional study trials.
limitations: All four experiments used college undergraduates and verbal paired-associate materials in a single laboratory session with only one 1-week retention interval.
qualityRationale: Four internally-replicated, randomly-assigned lab experiments with a delayed criterial test and a combined N of 320 support a Grade A controlled experimental study.

title: The effects of test trial and processing level on immediate and delayed retention
authors: Chang, S. H.
design: 2 (test trial: single vs. repeated) x 2 (processing level: shallow vs. deep) x 2 (recall timing: immediate vs. delayed) mixed-factorial experiment with random assignment to between-subject factors
population: College students, predominantly female, United States
outcome: Deep processing outperformed shallow processing on both immediate and delayed retention; single test trials showed a recall advantage over repeated trials on the immediate test but not on the delayed test, and additional study trials boosted delayed retention only for shallowly (not deeply) processed words.
limitations: The college-student sample and artificial word-list materials limit generalizability to authentic classroom learning.
qualityRationale: A peer-reviewed, randomly-assigned controlled lab experiment, but single-site with a modest sample (N=76), placing it at Grade B.

title: Forgetting rates of gist and peripheral episodic details in prose recall
authors: Sacripante, R., Logie, R. H., Baddeley, A. & Della Sala, S.
design: Three behavioural experiments using free recall of auditorily presented prose narratives, scored separately for central (gist) vs. secondary (peripheral) detail, tested at immediate and delayed intervals, with and without intermediate retrieval practice
population: Healthy young adults aged 18-35, native English speakers
outcome: Peripheral/secondary details were forgotten at a faster, negatively accelerated rate than central gist events; gist memory remained comparatively robust over time, and repeated retrieval benefited both memory types without eliminating the differential forgetting rate.
limitations: Lack of control over participants' expectations about the delayed recall test, inconsistent testing context across sessions, and variable intermediate-testing delays that may have added noise.
qualityRationale: Peer-reviewed, controlled multi-experiment lab study (3 experiments, N=232) with a replicated manipulation, but single-site in design.

title: Effect of levels-of-processing on rates of forgetting
authors: Peng, N., Logie, R. H. & Della Sala, S.
design: Three recognition-memory experiments manipulating encoding depth (semantic vs. shallow processing) with within- and between-participants designs, testing recognition accuracy at immediate and delayed intervals and fitting retention curves
population: Native English-speaking adults, primarily university students and online-platform participants
outcome: Deeper semantic processing produced superior recognition at both immediate and delayed test, but the slope/rate of forgetting did not differ significantly between deep and shallow processing conditions, indicating forgetting rate is independent of encoding depth.
limitations: Use of unrelated word lists as stimuli limits generalizability to naturalistic materials, and relatively short retention intervals were chosen to avoid floor effects.
qualityRationale: Peer-reviewed, controlled multi-experiment lab study (3 experiments, N=282) manipulating encoding depth directly, but not a randomized multisite trial.

title: Reductions in Retrieval Competition Predict the Benefit of Repeated Testing
authors: Rafidi, N. S., Hulbert, J. C., Brooks, P. P. & Norman, K. A.
design: Three-session EEG experiment: session 1 established a neural competition classifier via a semantic-category retrieval localizer; session 2 had participants study/test novel Swahili-English vocabulary; session 3 (one week later) tested delayed recall, correlating trial-by-trial competition reduction with later retention
population: Right-handed, native English-speaking adults with normal/corrected vision and no prior Swahili knowledge
institution: Princeton University; Carnegie Mellon University; Bard College
outcome: The degree to which neural competition decreased for a given vocabulary word across retrieval-practice attempts predicted whether that word was successfully remembered one week later, supporting a retrieval-competition-reduction account of why testing improves long-term retention over restudy.
limitations: Cannot fully disentangle competition from item difficulty, no restudy-only control condition was included, and EEG signal was too noisy to support real-time trial-by-trial feedback.
qualityRationale: Peer-reviewed controlled experimental lab study with a within-subject manipulation and objective (EEG) neural measures, though sample size is modest (N=40) and single-site.

title: A critical period for second language acquisition: Evidence from 2/3 million English speakers
authors: Hartshorne, J. K., Tenenbaum, J. B. & Pinker, S.
design: Large-scale web-based grammaticality-judgment game with a computational model disentangling current age, age of first exposure, and years of experience, applied to a very large observational dataset
population: Native and non-native English speakers of all ages, self-selected online game participants worldwide
institution: Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Harvard University
outcome: Grammar-learning ability for a second language is preserved almost until the cusp of adulthood (about 17.4 years) and then declines steadily; this held for both syntactically difficult and easy phenomena, indicating a sharply defined critical/sensitive period for language-learning capacity.
limitations: Data come from a self-selected online sample rather than a randomly sampled or controlled population, and exposure history and age of first exposure are self-reported.
qualityRationale: Large-scale (N≈670,000) primary dataset study with a novel computational design that addresses prior underpowering, published in a major peer-reviewed journal.

title: Investigating the Effects of Spacing on Working Memory Training Outcome: A Randomized, Controlled, Multisite Trial in Older Adults
authors: Jaeggi, S. M., Buschkuehl, M., Parlett-Pelleriti, C. M., Moon, S. M., Evans, M., Kritzmacher, A., Reuter-Lorenz, P. A., Shah, P. & Jonides, J.
design: Randomized controlled multisite trial with a 2 (working-memory training vs. active knowledge-training control) x 3 (twice-daily, once-daily, every-other-day spacing) design, tested at baseline, post-intervention, and 3-month follow-up
population: Healthy older adults recruited from Southern California and Southeast Michigan
venue: The Journals of Gerontology: Series B (Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences)
institution: University of California, Irvine; University of Michigan
outcome: Working-memory training produced modest transfer effects sustained at 3-month follow-up in older adults, but the spacing of training sessions affected learning gains only minimally, contrary to the spacing-effect hypothesis for this population.
limitations: Pre-post assessment intervals differed across spacing conditions, the range of spacing conditions tested was restricted, and there was no no-contact control group to rule out test-retest effects.
qualityRationale: Randomized, controlled, multisite trial with an active control condition and follow-up assessment in a defined older-adult population.

title: Building Digital Literacy in Older Adults of Low Socioeconomic Status in Singapore (Project Wire Up): Nonrandomized Controlled Trial
authors: Ngiam, N. H. W., Yee, W. Q., Teo, N., Yow, K. S., Soundararajan, A., Lim, J. X., Lim, H. A., Tey, A., Tang, K. W. A., Tham, C. Y. X., Tan, J. P. Y., Lu, S. Y., Yoon, S., Ng, K. Y. Y. & Low, L. L.
design: Nonrandomized, waitlist-controlled trial providing smartphones, cellular data, and volunteer-led digital-skills training to an intervention group, compared against a waitlist control group, measured pre/post over a defined study period
population: Community-dwelling adults aged 55+ of lower socioeconomic status in Singapore, living in public rental housing or receiving public assistance
institution: TriGen (Trigenerational Homecare); Singapore General Hospital / SingHealth
outcome: The intervention group showed significantly greater improvement in digital literacy scores than the waitlist control group, though no significant secondary-outcome differences emerged for loneliness, social connectedness, quality of life, or subjective well-being.
limitations: Nonrandom group assignment, self-reported outcome measures prone to bias, and differing follow-up timeframes between groups.
qualityRationale: Peer-reviewed, prospective controlled (waitlist) intervention trial with a defined older, low-SES population, though allocation was nonrandom.

title: The "practical significance" of Locke's theory of goal setting
authors: Latham, G. P. & Baldes, J. J.
design: Field quasi-experiment (ABA time-series) manipulating goal specificity/difficulty (assigned hard load-weight goal vs. prior 'do your best' instruction) with truck-load weight tracked over 12 consecutive months
population: Logging truck drivers across six logging operations, Pacific Northwest USA
outcome: Assigning a specific, difficult goal produced an immediate and sustained increase in the percentage of legal net weight hauled compared to the prior vague 'do your best' period.
limitations: Single-organization field study with no randomized control group; the goal-setting condition was introduced together with public record-keeping/feedback, so goal specificity is partly confounded with increased feedback visibility.
qualityRationale: Real-world quasi-experimental field study manipulating goal specificity with objective operational outcome data over many months, though it lacks random assignment or a concurrent control group.

title: Effects of feedback sign and credibility on goal setting and task performance
authors: Podsakoff, P. M. & Farh, J.-L.
design: Randomized laboratory experiment, 2 (feedback sign: positive/negative) x 2 (feedback credibility: high/low) between-subjects factorial design on an idea-generation task with subsequent self-set goals
population: Undergraduate business students at a US university
venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
outcome: Participants who received more credible negative feedback set higher subsequent goals and performed better than those who received less credible negative feedback; feedback credibility had little effect on goals or performance following positive feedback.
limitations: Single-session laboratory task using an artificial idea-generation exercise, limiting generalizability to sustained, real-world learning or performance-feedback contexts.
qualityRationale: Randomized between-subjects laboratory experiment manipulating feedback sign and credibility with measured goal-setting and performance outcomes.

title: Impact of process and outcome feedback on the relation of goal setting to task performance
authors: Earley, P. C., Northcraft, G. B., Lee, C. & Lituchy, T. R.
design: Randomized laboratory experiment with a fully crossed factorial design (goal setting x process feedback x outcome feedback) using a repeated-trial stock-investment computer simulation
population: University business students performing a simulated investment task
institution: University of Minnesota; University of Arizona
outcome: Process feedback combined with goal setting was more strongly related to information-search quality and task strategy than outcome feedback; outcome feedback combined with goal setting was more strongly related to self-confidence and effort.
limitations: Single-session laboratory task using a simulated investment game; findings distinguishing process vs. outcome feedback may not generalize to classroom or applied skill-learning settings.
qualityRationale: Randomized factorial laboratory experiment isolating process vs. outcome feedback effects on the goal-performance relationship with objective task-performance measures.

title: HabitWalk: A micro-randomized trial to understand and promote habit formation in physical activity
authors: Baretta, D., Gillmann, N., Edgren, R. & Inauen, J.
design: Micro-randomized trial (7-day preparatory phase + 105-day experimental phase) with daily randomization of 'commitment' and 'prompts and cues' behavior-change techniques delivered via a walking-habit mobile app, with daily self-reported habit strength and tracker-measured steps
population: Adults seeking to increase walking/physical activity, recruited via app, Switzerland
outcome: Cue-behavior repetition positively predicted subsequent habit strength within persons (but habit strength did not predict later repetition); combining commitment and prompts/cues techniques was tentatively supported as a habit-promotion strategy.
limitations: Very small sample (N=24) limits statistical power and generalizability; participants were self-selected app users already motivated to build a walking habit.
qualityRationale: Micro-randomized trial design with daily within-person randomization and 105 days of intensive objective step tracking provides strong causal inference despite the small sample.

title: The impact of reminders on implementation intention: A randomized controlled trial
authors: Messmer, L., Fenouillet, F. & Legrand, E.
design: 2 (implementation intention: present/absent) x 2 (reminder: present/absent) x 4 (week) repeated-measures randomized controlled trial testing whether text-message reminders sustain the effect of implementation intentions on daily self-set goal completion over four weeks
population: Adults in France during COVID-19 lockdown who set and reported daily goals via a dedicated website
outcome: Implementation intentions and reminders each had significant main effects on sustained daily goal follow-through, but reminders did not significantly amplify (interact with) the implementation-intention effect over the four weeks.
limitations: Substantial attrition (194 recruited, 118 analyzed), reliance on self-reported goal completion via website, and data collected under atypical COVID-19 lockdown conditions.
qualityRationale: Randomized 2x2 factorial controlled trial with a four-week repeated-measures design directly testing a cue/reminder-based intervention on sustained goal-directed return behavior, though with notable attrition and self-report outcomes.
