title: Creating Exercise Habits Using Incentives: The Trade-off Between Flexibility and Routinization
authors: Beshears, J., Lee, H. N., Milkman, K. L., Mislavsky, R. & Wisdom, J.
design: Randomized field experiment comparing routine-based incentives (paid only for gym visits within a fixed daily two-hour window) vs. flexible incentives (paid for any gym visit) for building exercise habits, with a follow-up period after incentives were removed to test persistence/return
population: Employees of a Fortune 500 company with access to an on-site/company-affiliated gym, USA
institution: Harvard Business School; The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania
outcome: Flexible incentives produced more gym visits than routine-based incentives, both during the incentive period and afterward; routinizing the behavior around a fixed daily window did not improve habit persistence relative to flexible timing.
limitations: Single-employer field sample tied to a financial-incentive paradigm; post-incentive persistence effect sizes were modest, and habit/return behavior was inferred from gym check-in records rather than direct automaticity measures.
qualityRationale: Large-scale (N=2,508) randomized field experiment with objective behavioral tracking directly testing competing habit-formation/return interventions and their post-intervention persistence.

title: Testing the testing effect in the classroom
authors: McDaniel, M. A., Anderson, J. L., Derbish, M. H. & Morrisette, N.
design: Quasi-experimental field study embedded in a real undergraduate course; topics were randomly assigned across six counterbalanced quiz-format/reading conditions within subjects
population: Undergraduate students enrolled in a web-based college 'Brain and Behavior' course
outcome: Weekly short-answer and multiple-choice quizzes (but not equivalent additional reading) significantly improved later unit-test and cumulative final-exam performance on quizzed material relative to non-quizzed material; short-answer quizzes produced larger gains than multiple-choice quizzes.
limitations: Single course, single site, modest completer sample (N=35) with voluntary extra-credit participation, which may limit generalizability and introduce self-selection.
qualityRationale: Peer-reviewed controlled field experiment with randomized counterbalancing of topic/quiz-format in an authentic college course, but single-site with a modest sample size.

title: Repeated testing improves long-term retention relative to repeated study: a randomised controlled trial
authors: Larsen, D. P., Butler, A. C. & Roediger, H. L., III
design: Randomized controlled trial with a counterbalanced, within-subjects crossover design (each resident tested on one topic and studied the other)
population: Pediatric and emergency medicine residents attending a didactic teaching conference
outcome: At more than 6 months after the initial teaching session, repeated short-answer testing with feedback produced final test scores 13 percentage points higher than repeated studying of equivalent material.
limitations: Small, single-site sample (N=40) of residents at one institution, and only two medical topics were tested, limiting generalizability across content domains.
qualityRationale: Randomized controlled trial with a counterbalanced crossover design in an authentic clinical-education setting, measured at an educationally meaningful 6-month retention interval.

title: The spacing effect in children's memory and category induction
authors: Vlach, H. A., Sandhofer, C. M. & Kornell, N.
design: Controlled lab experiment, 2 (presentation style: massed vs. spaced; within-subjects) x 2 (task: memory vs. category induction; between-subjects) design
population: Three-year-old children recruited from preschools in the Los Angeles area
outcome: Spaced presentation of novel object/category instances produced significantly better performance on delayed multiple-choice memory and category-induction tests than massed presentation, despite spacing making the immediate task harder.
limitations: Small, single-site sample of preschool-recruited children, and the task measured near-term multiple-choice recognition of simplified artificial stimuli rather than long-term applied learning.
qualityRationale: Peer-reviewed controlled experiment with random assignment and a within-subjects spacing manipulation, but a small, single-site developmental sample.

title: Spacing Simultaneously Promotes Multiple Forms of Learning in Children's Science Curriculum
authors: Gluckman, M., Vlach, H. A. & Sandhofer, C. M.
design: Randomized, controlled between-subjects experiment (massed vs. clumped vs. spaced lesson schedules) embedded in a science-curriculum intervention, with a 1-week delayed test
population: Early-elementary school-aged children recruited from a university laboratory school
institution: University of California, Los Angeles; University of Wisconsin-Madison
outcome: At a 1-week delayed test, children who received science lessons on a spaced schedule showed significantly better memory and generalization than children in massed or clumped conditions; no significant relationship was found between memory and generalization performance.
limitations: Small per-cell sample (n=12 per condition, 9 additional children excluded for non-completion) from a single laboratory school, limiting statistical power and generalizability.
qualityRationale: Randomized controlled classroom-embedded experiment testing an authentic science curriculum, but a small per-cell sample size at a single site limits power and generalizability.
